I never put a review, but Naraka is a kind of game I've been looking for for a while. Despite it full of bots, I still find it quite fun. Until you reach around Solar rank, expect to have lobby's with only bots. If you're someone who likes to learn about mechanics, high skill ceiling gameplay, rock-paper-scissors/movement combat, competitive, and don't mind much about the bots, then this game is definitely worth a try. PVE (rift traversal): I started off with the PVE aspects of the game, and there's not much of a player base in it. There are secrets and cool puzzles, but I had to look up how to do it because the game doesn't give you much time to figure it out unless if you replay the mission again and again. I find that the losing all your equipment can be pretty punishing especially since there is so much need for rare materials to get the equipment do the perilous or doomed paths. They give you free lo tier equipment, but as someone who isn't on the game 24/7, I can't spend my time on the PVE too much. *This game is meant for PVP. There is plenty of content for PVE, but I only really do it for the event rewards.* The gameplay and potential of the game is why I'm giving this game a good review. The community in-game felt very inviting, and everyone just seems to have the same interest(to play with people lol). Fighting games is already a niche genre, but personally this game really deserves more recognition. PS: Needs a west coast NA server

Path of Exile is an outstanding free-to-play action RPG that delivers an incredibly deep and demanding adventure through a world consumed by darkness, corruption, and supernatural horrors. Developed and published by Grinding Gear Games, it distinguishes itself through extraordinary character customization, challenging combat, and an enormous collection of interconnected progression systems. Set on the hostile continent of Wraeclast, the game places players in the role of an exile fighting to survive against terrifying creatures and powerful adversaries. Its greatest achievement is the freedom it provides to experiment with different playstyles, although that same complexity can make the experience intimidating for newcomers. For players who appreciate intricate mechanics and long-term character development, it offers one of the most substantial experiences available in the genre. The atmosphere immediately establishes a grim and unforgiving identity. Abandoned settlements, corrupted wildernesses, ancient ruins, and grotesque monsters create a convincing world where danger feels ever-present. The narrative gradually reveals the disturbing history of Wraeclast through quests, dialogue, environmental storytelling, and encounters with memorable characters. Although the lore is extensive and fascinating, its presentation sometimes takes a secondary role to relentless combat and equipment progression. Nevertheless, the dark fantasy setting remains compelling, supported by excellent environmental design, unsettling sound effects, and atmospheric music that reinforces the feeling of exploring a civilization devastated by supernatural forces. Combat is fast, destructive, and remarkably flexible. Players can specialize in melee attacks, ranged weapons, elemental spells, summoned allies, traps, and numerous unconventional combinations. Defeating large groups of enemies with carefully developed abilities creates an immensely satisfying sense of power, while challenging bosses demand awareness, preparation, and appropriate defensive strategies. The skill gem system is particularly impressive because abilities can be modified through support gems, allowing seemingly ordinary attacks to evolve into devastating combinations. However, encounters can become visually chaotic when numerous projectiles and effects overwhelm the screen. Certain character builds also encourage repetitive ability usage, making extended grinding sessions occasionally monotonous. Character progression represents the game's most distinctive accomplishment. Its enormous passive skill tree provides an astonishing degree of freedom, allowing players to construct highly specialized characters without being completely restricted by traditional class identities. Ascendancy specializations introduce additional layers of customization, while equipment modifiers and skill interactions create countless opportunities for experimentation. Discovering effective combinations can be incredibly rewarding, especially when a carefully planned build begins overcoming previously impossible challenges. Unfortunately, the learning curve is exceptionally steep. Newcomers may struggle to understand complicated mechanics, and poorly distributed passive points can significantly weaken a character. The game rewards research and patience but offers comparatively little forgiveness for inexperienced decisions. Equipment acquisition and crafting provide another compelling foundation for progression. Defeated enemies frequently drop weapons, armor, accessories, and valuable crafting materials, encouraging constant experimentation with different combinations of attributes. The unconventional currency system gives numerous resources practical crafting functions, creating a fascinating relationship between item improvement and trading. Finding a rare piece of equipment or successfully crafting a powerful upgrade can feel genuinely exciting. However, randomized outcomes occasionally make progression frustrating, particularly when substantial resources disappear without producing worthwhile improvements. Inventory management also becomes increasingly demanding as players accumulate enormous quantities of equipment and specialized materials. The endgame offers exceptional longevity through the Atlas of Worlds, challenging maps, formidable bosses, and numerous specialized activities. Completing the main campaign opens the door to increasingly sophisticated progression systems that encourage players to refine their characters and pursue more difficult encounters. Challenge leagues further enhance replayability by introducing fresh mechanics and opportunities to begin new adventures. These features make the game particularly appealing to dedicated players who enjoy optimization and continuous improvement. However, the sheer amount of available content can feel overwhelming, and reaching the highest levels of progression often requires considerable grinding and detailed mechanical knowledge. Multiplayer adds another dimension through cooperative encounters, trading, and community interaction. Players can collaborate against dangerous enemies or participate in an extensive economy where valuable equipment and crafting resources are exchanged. The game also supports independent progression, although a persistent internet connection remains necessary. Its free-to-play model is commendable because the core adventure and substantial endgame content are accessible without mandatory purchases. Most optional transactions involve cosmetics, while additional stash tabs provide meaningful storage convenience. These purchases are not required to enjoy the campaign, but dedicated players may find them increasingly useful. From a technical perspective, the game delivers impressive environmental detail, distinctive monster designs, and spectacular combat effects. Its visual presentation successfully captures the brutality of its setting, although performance can fluctuate during encounters involving numerous enemies and elaborate abilities. Steam Deck compatibility is officially rated Playable, meaning the game can be enjoyed on Valve's handheld system but is not fully Verified. Controller support makes combat accessible, although navigating complicated menus, managing inventory, and examining detailed equipment descriptions can feel cumbersome on the smaller display. Graphically demanding encounters may also require reduced settings for smoother performance. Ultimately, Path of Exile is a remarkable achievement in action RPG design, offering exceptional customization, rewarding combat, and almost overwhelming replayability. Its greatest weaknesses are its intimidating complexity, occasional performance problems, demanding inventory management, and reliance on repetitive grinding. Nevertheless, these shortcomings rarely diminish the satisfaction of mastering its elaborate systems and developing increasingly powerful characters. It is particularly recommended for players who enjoy strategic character building, challenging encounters, and extensive endgame progression. Those seeking a casual adventure may find its demands exhausting, but dedicated enthusiasts will discover an extraordinarily rewarding experience. Rating: 9/10

I just bought Conan Exiles Enhanced with all DLCs, and I was shocked by how much I loved the game, especially since I had never heard of it before. Which is actually strange, because I’ve thoroughly enjoyed many Funcom games - starting with Anarchy Online (which was revolutionary for its time), the one with the Illuminati and secret societies (the first game that didn't send me off to gather 5 rat tails, and where I truly enjoyed the puzzles and deep skill customization), and, of course, the first Conan with that amazing Tortage Island. Gosh, I loved that island! So how did I completely miss this brilliant game with its engaging combat system, intriguing lore, and wonderful open-world environment built on Unreal Engine 5? Life, I guess? Job, wife, kid, plus 150+ (bought and unplayed) games on Steam alone. What I like most is the flexibility Funcom gives us: we can play online in PvE or PvP... OR... we can play as a single-player RPG with full server admin rights! You can modify everything from stamina consumption, day and night lengths, and equipment durability to hunger and thirst mechanics. Remember how mods transformed Skyrim or Fallout into survival games? This is the exact opposite: a survival game that can be tweaked to play like a traditional RPG at any point during your playthrough. Wow, Funcom, sincerely, THANKS. What I'd love to see added or improved: 1. A expanded map for the Exiled Lands (the original world) -that would be amazing. 2. Facial animations: Since the game was upgraded to Unreal Engine 5, some lip-syncing would make a huge difference. Nowadays, it feels strange to talk to Conan without his lips moving. 3. NPC AI updates: As I write this, I’m stuck between my follower, two barrels, and a wall in Klael's Stronghold, which suddenly brought back vivid memories of poor Lydia and Rog-Wo-Dah. Move, woman! UPDATE: luckily a skeleton respawned and attacked my companion setting me free. Good job Klael.

NARAKA: BLADEPOINT — I Came for the Combat, Stayed for the Fashion, and Forgot How Clocks Work 784 hours played. 32 days and 16 hours of my life. Zero regrets. Mostly. I've spent 784 hours playing NARAKA: BLADEPOINT, so I think I've earned the right to talk about it. Is it enough time to master the game? Probably not. Is it enough time to develop an unhealthy attachment to virtual cosmetics? Absolutely. NARAKA combines fast-paced melee combat, incredible mobility, beautiful character designs, tons of events, and enough content to keep you busy for an alarming amount of time. You launch the game thinking, "I'll play for 30 minutes." Three hours later, your dinner is cold, your sleep schedule has filed a missing person report, and you're saying, "Just one more match." Welcome to NARAKA. Character Customization: The REAL Endgame The character customization system offers plenty of options for facial features, hairstyles, colors, and other details. Add the gorgeous skins, outfits, and accessories, and you've got a recipe for disaster. A very beautiful disaster. Seriously, the art team deserves a raise. You can spend hours creating the perfect character, adjusting every little detail until everything looks just right. Then you finish and realize you haven't actually played the game. Your enemies are practicing combos. You're studying color theory. They're preparing for battle. You're preparing a fashion show. And somehow, you're having the time of your life. After 784 hours, there's always another character to customize or another tiny detail that MUST be changed. At this point, NARAKA is two games in a trench coat: a combat game and a character customization simulator. And I'm not sure which one I'm better at. Events Everywhere! (Goodbye, Free Time) NARAKA does a great job with events and seasonal content. There's always something to do, from completing missions to unlocking cosmetics. You log in to complete your daily missions. Easy, right? Wrong. You notice an event, check the rewards, discover another mission, and spot a skin you absolutely need. Suddenly, your original plan is gone, your bedtime is in danger, and you're doing missions you didn't even know existed five minutes ago. Daily missions aren't missions anymore. They're a legally binding contract. You don't log in to play. You report for duty. Congratulations, NARAKA. You've reinvented unpaid overtime. The Battle Pass: Your Wallet Is Safe. Your Free Time Isn't. You can purchase the Battle Pass with Gold and earn all that Gold back by completing all 115 levels . Finish the pass, recover your Gold, and put it toward the next one. Save it, and you can keep the cycle going without spending real money on every new pass. Your wallet: "Finally, some peace and quiet." Your free time: "I've been sacrificed for the greater good." There's just one small detail: you have to complete all 115 levels. The Gold comes back. The hours don't. Considering I've already played for 784 hours, I'm probably not the right person to ask for time-management advice. Playing With Friends: Friendship Is Temporary, Chaos Is Eternal Playing with friends makes NARAKA even more fun. You can coordinate attacks, develop strategies, and save each other from terrible situations. Of course, that assumes anyone remembers the plan once the first enemy appears. One person is fighting, another is running in the opposite direction, and someone is asking what just happened. Teamwork makes the dream work. Unfortunately, nobody told the team what the dream was. Winning together feels great, but sometimes the funniest matches are the ones where absolutely everything goes wrong. RNG: Random Number Generator or Personal Enemy? Trying to get a specific cosmetic can be painful. You know exactly what you want, open your rewards full of hope, and the game gives you literally anything else. You try again. More disappointment. Again. Nothing. At this point, you're conducting a scientific experiment on the relationship between hope and suffering. You start wondering whether the game knows exactly what you want and deliberately avoids giving it to you. When you finally get something amazing, it feels fantastic. Until then, you're questioning your luck and possibly the entire mathematical foundation of the universe. You close the menu and reconsider your life choices. Then you open it again. Because apparently, we never learn. After 784 hours, I've concluded that RNG and I have a complicated relationship. I want the cosmetics. RNG wants me to suffer. It's not healthy, but I'm too invested to leave. So, Is NARAKA: BLADEPOINT Worth Playing? Absolutely. The combat is exciting, the customization is extensive, the skins are gorgeous, the events keep things fresh, and playing with friends makes everything better. Sure, RNG can be frustrating, but it doesn't take away from how enjoyable the game is overall. If you enjoy action games, collecting cosmetics, customizing characters, and playing with friends, NARAKA is absolutely worth checking out. Just be warned. You start playing for the combat. You stay for the cosmetics. You spend an hour customizing a character, get distracted by an event, complete your daily missions, play with friends, and get wrecked by RNG. Then you look at the clock and say: "Okay, just one more match." Congratulations. You've officially become part of the problem. 784 hours played. 32 days and 16 hours gone. Still playing. I could have learned a new language or become a responsible adult. Instead, I learned that the perfect shade of blue matters, daily missions are legally binding, and RNG is my natural enemy. Would I do it all again? Absolutely. 10/10 — Would lose track of time again. Your wallet is safe. Your free time, however, is another story. Send help. Or Gold. Preferably Gold.

I already had this game for PS Vita and I love it just as much on PC. Imagine a game that is a hybrid of turn based dungeon crawler RPG and sports team management sim. You constantly recruit and manage your team of adventurers, rotate them out and ensure their well being while they progress and develop both positive and negative traits. Death is permanent so ensuring that you have plenty of capable party members waiting in reserve is crucial. If you enjoy both adventuring as well as tweaking and managing stats this game is going to be right up your alley. You will find what archetypes complement each other and what strategies to build your different parties around. The game can be punishingly difficult at times (at least for me it was) and will test your resolve and management skills.

A Different Side of Watch Dogs Watch Dogs 2 is one of those games that makes you appreciate how much personality an open world can have. Coming back to the series after the first game, it's interesting to see how different the sequel feels while still keeping what made the original enjoyable. San Francisco is a fantastic setting, full of life, colour and things to discover. Exploring the city never really gets old, and the soundtrack fits the atmosphere brilliantly, giving the game its own identity and making the world feel alive. One of my favourite parts is the story and the DedSec crew. The characters each have their own personalities, and their interactions bring plenty of humour and charm. Although the tone is much lighter than the first game, the story still explores interesting ideas about privacy, surveillance and the power of technology. It makes you want to see what happens next. The gameplay is another highlight. The hacking mechanics give you plenty of freedom in how you approach missions, while the RC Jumper and Quadcopter make things even more enjoyable. Experimenting with different approaches keeps the gameplay fresh throughout. Of course, the game isn't perfect. Some of the humour doesn't always land, and parts of the story feel a little uneven, but these issues don't take away from the overall experience. Overall, Watch Dogs 2 is a brilliant sequel that takes the series in a different direction and makes it work. With a memorable cast, an incredible setting and entertaining gameplay, it's a game that's easy to get lost in. text_clean: Look. I know pointing to my playtime and walking away is lazy, but like...what more do you want from me? It's the 1999 classic in all its glory but with a support level on par with any modern game. You can reasonably criticize the idea to upend certain long-standing gameplay systems with more recent patches and expansions, but at its core it still hits all the nostalgia notes while also allowing the growth that comes from 25+ years of game and map design evolution. And some of the newer, longer story campaigns from Chronicles or the recent Viking Sagas show that the underlying engine can power vastly different ideas than whatever was envisioned back then. Like, I can play a complicated, 12-hour scenario full of triggers and conditions, with all the polish of a major studio, but I can also still play basically the same scenarios I played on my Pentium III when I was 15. Or I can just comp-stomp and vibe to the soundtrack. More than any of the other Definitive Editions, it's a platform for both memories and modern development.

好玩，不卡利用bug慢慢去玩是很有意思的，我很喜欢这种慢慢积攒材料搭建生产线路，完善加工环境来达成高的价值产出，且本游戏产出的货币不像别的工厂产线类型游戏一样只是数值或成就，我认为这个游戏主要部分是探索建造，探索需要钱建造需要材料，所以赋予了这些材料产线极大的意义，探索部分我认为已经相当成熟了，可以探索的内容非常之多，玩家可以通过不断地探索拿到仅属于自己与众不同且稀有的飞船，武器，宠物，这让我很有成就感，产线搭建完善后拥有足够的建筑材料后搭建各种好看的建筑也非常有趣，整条游戏路程下来游玩自己所发现的所得到的所创造的所走过的路让我有一种说不出来的成就感，太空环境星系探险做的非常棒，以上这些都是建立在不利用bug锁生存模式才有的体会，再多人方面，当在探索的过程中遇到别人留下的建筑或者留言，在这个游戏的剧情背景下让我深刻的感受到那句话，“你不是孤身一人”这种设定非常沉浸，新的联盟系统更是可以把和朋友们一起努力探索发现的东西量化，更直观的看到我和朋友在这个游戏中获得的成就。以上是我认为的优点，但是我看了本游戏的一些宣发视频，我感觉官方后续更新可能不会很多了，这让我有些失落，因为我觉得还可以完善很多东西，例如此游戏的boss怪物太少了，我们拿到了很厉害的武器很厉害的飞船但是没有用武之地，联盟的竞争属性我认为也存在很大问题，我觉得游戏方应该多鼓励认认真真玩不卡bug不开修改器的玩家，现在的联盟排名囊括了所有类型玩家，锁生存不卡bug的玩家不可能和开着修改器或创造模式的玩家竞争。另外游戏的生存要素较少，最重要的就是bug太多了，如果这个游戏bug能少一点，没有那么多恶性bug就会是最棒的沙盒探索游戏，例如精炼机复制bug，这个bug真的很尴尬，有这个bug在可以说我搭建的各种产线都是无意义的，虽然可以说靠自觉不用，但是大多数玩家都在用的这种环境下，多少给真正好好玩的玩家有一定的落差感，不是一定要修复所有bug而是尽可能不要出现影响游戏的恶性bug，这个bug存在很久了一直没有修复，我认为这很影响游玩心态，另一方面我认为游戏应该继续完善一下材料生产部分，本游戏如果不卡bug这些材料产线我认为是很有必要的，但是目前的产线没有任何自动化成分，只是让材料能固定产出，而合成精炼部分没有自动化产线的功能，可能达成那种核融起爆机自动量产产线很难，但是起码精炼部分我认为可以完善一下，在货船加入自动精炼物品的功能，或许可以设计成那种控制面板例如货船内部装一个新的工作房间，这个工作房间可以统一调控货船上已有的精炼机，玩家设定好配方以及最低保有量后开始批量自动精炼，现在我每次缺钱都要一直反复机械的在熔炉里操作一个小时，另外我们需要更好的二氢产出路线。

Hands down the best Civ entry and that's kind of painful to write in 2026 when we have two newer entries, but it's a fact. This was the entry that started the hex based single unit phase and it was an amazing change. War felt strategic where in previous entries you'd just throw doomstacks back and forth. This is also the last time the game actually focused on the Civilizations. Civilization 6 and 7 leaned way to hard into historical leaders. Building cities and developing your lands was also peak with this game. 6 spilled the cities out onto the map which made no sense since we've only urbanized about 3% of available land on Earth even today. That and they went crazy with adjacency bonuses in 6 and made them even worse in 7. They don't feel like civilization anymore, they feel more like a dorfromantic style map puzzler. Until a different team of developers gets to make a new entry, or a true competitor comes out of nowhere the way Cities Skylines knocked out Sim City, this is the turn based historical sim you're looking for.

Watch Dogs 2 is a pretty decent game and I had a good time playing it, but I wouldn't call it anything special. The story is okay, the characters are interesting enough, and the open world is fun to explore at first, but the game has quite a few problems that keep it from being great. One of the best things about the game is definitely the main missions. There are some genuinely fun moments, and Robot Wars was easily my favorite mission in the entire game. It was creative, entertaining, and actually felt different from the usual missions. Unfortunately, most of the other missions follow pretty much the same formula: break into a building, hack something, get the information you need, and leave. The hacking itself is fun initially, especially when you use drones and different gadgets to avoid enemies, but it gets repetitive after a while. I really wish there were more types of hacking mechanics and more variety in how you approach objectives. I also tried a few side missions, but honestly, most of them were pretty trash and didn't really motivate me to keep playing them. The open world has plenty of activities, but quantity doesn't always mean quality. The characters are decent, and Ray was easily my favorite. He has a lot of personality and brings some entertaining moments to the story. Dusan, on the other hand, reminded me a bit of Joseph Seed from Far Cry 5, both in appearance and behavior. The story itself is okay, but I never found it particularly amazing or memorable. Driving isn't bad either, and the cars handle well enough, but I barely used them because fast travel was simply more convenient. I honestly don't think I've ever gone somewhere without using fast travel unless a mission forced me to drive. The city looks great, though, and exploring San Francisco is enjoyable, especially with all the hacking opportunities and things you can interact with. I also like that the game gives you different ways to approach certain situations. You can sneak around, use your gadgets, distract enemies, or go in more aggressively if things go wrong. Playing stealthily and using your tools creatively can be really satisfying, even if the underlying objectives start feeling repetitive. Overall, Watch Dogs 2 is worth playing, especially if you enjoy open-world games and messing around with hacking mechanics. It has some great moments, likable characters, and a fun setting, but the repetitive missions and underwhelming side content hold it back. It's a good enough game, just not one I'd consider particularly memorable. For me, the first Watch Dogs is still clearly superior, especially in terms of story, atmosphere, and the overall experience. Watch Dogs 2 is more colorful and playful, but I personally prefer the darker tone of the original. Final verdict: 7/10. A fun game that's worth trying, but it could have been so much better with more mission variety and a stronger story.

A masterclass in blending roguelite and Metroidvania into something that feels both fresh and endlessly replayable. The combat is the star here: fast, fluid, and brutally satisfying, with every dodge, parry, and weapon combination feeling weighty and responsive . The pixel art is gorgeous, the soundtrack slaps, and the progression system—unlocking new weapons and permanent upgrades between runs—keeps you coming back even after a hundred deaths . The caveats are real: it's punishing, and the difficulty curve after the first clear is a genuine wall that demands patience and practice . Some weapons feel unbalanced, and the early biomes can get repetitive after dozens of hours . But with 97% positive Steam reviews from over 130,000 players and multiple Game of the Year awards, this is essential for anyone who loves action games that respect your skill . Just be ready to die. A lot.

在我的青春回忆里，《方舟：生存进化》几乎填满了我大部分闲暇时光。我与方舟的故事，要从 2019 年说起。17 岁那年，拥有了属于自己的电脑，偶然遇到了这款游戏，开放的史前世界深深吸引了我，我毫不犹豫入了坑。 第一次进游戏，是单人孤岛地图。眼前的一切都无比新鲜，仿佛真的穿越到侏罗纪。意外捶晕的一头三角龙，成为了我的第一只恐龙。骑着它一路探索到沼泽，被泰坦巨蟒吓得慌忙跑路。期间也建造了个小基地，也就三五块地基大小。 后来我试着去服务器游玩，裸连进不去官服，就随便进了一个私服 ——3643 仙境。我加入一个了部落，首领教我怎么用阿根廷巨鹰抓起甲龙，让我没事就带甲龙去打铁 哈哈，现在看来那不就是小黑奴嘛，。但部落里的人都很友善，我在这里认识了同期入部的好友 SHU。我的 ID 是 SUN，我们二人相约来到孤岛月牙岛的双尖，一人占一块地，各自搭建起经典的大号火柴盒基地。 可惜美好的时光没能持续多久，这个私服关服了。SHU 转战官服，我另找了一个私服，遇见萌新枯叶。有过上一个私服温暖的经历，我也耐心带着枯叶一起开荒：驯龙、挑战 BOSS，还打算修建一座宫殿，只可惜最后烂尾了。 再之后枯叶也去往官服，我便跟着一同前往。此时枯叶在官服已经经营起规模不小的部落，还有铭书、大肠、爱等一众伙伴。那几年恰逢疫情，大家都有大把时间聚在游戏里，闲暇时也会在群里聊聊现实生活。创世纪 2 上线后，我去到 SHU 所在的 924 服务器安家，算是我们部落的一个分部。偶尔我还会跑到 SHU 家里 “顺手” 摸点物资和恐龙。 那时候一开游戏就能玩上一整天。哪怕到后期所有 BOSS 都已经通关，我依旧会上线，骑着喜欢的恐龙四处漫游。直到官服即将关停的消息传来，心里满是不舍。那是我在侏罗纪世界里的家啊。大家日夜搭建的建筑即将消失，还有一只只从小养起的恐龙，只能永远沉睡在低温仓中了。我的青春时光，也一同留在了这片方舟大陆……

Probably going against the grain with a downvote here... maybe a me-problem? but anyway. Is this a bad game? Maybe not objectively. Graphics style is cool, the controls feel fast and responsive, and it's got a whole lot of content. Music is manageable, but not memorable. But am I having fun playing this? To be honest, not particularly. It's a combination of things. Just to ramble a bit: - The game is designed to be grindy by design. You have to unlock every f--ing thing. If that's what keeps if interesting for you, sure. Otherwise: eh. It's really one big grind-a-thon, The roguelite genre taken to extremes. - There may be a story somewhere, but i was just some headless dude fighting through dungeons until i killed a king. And then I was back at the start. Some vague lore drops are dropped here and there, but i didn't really care about it since it was never presented in a way that made me care. Or something. - Then you traverse a whole corridor only to find out you don't have the permanent upgrade unlocked that is required to keep going that way. Or worse, it leads to a door and when you try to enter it it says "DLC REQUIRED". Please. - Partly a skill issue, but the combat system never really clicked for me either. When going 1 on 1, it's usually okay, but when it gets more frenzied a lot of stuff can be going on at the screen especially with gibs and effects. This can lead to bs like (for example) make it hard to see enemy projectiles. At the end of it all, the core gameplay loop doesn't seem to reward much other than feeding into itself for the sake of it. And I never really had that "just one more try" moment that some games give. I might throw a few more runs in after this review. But I don't expect it to cause me to drastically change my opinion from this.

A little while ago I was obsessed with a game called no skin. It was a horror Roguelike that really took me for a ride, so much so that I made the effort to 100% it which is rare for me. Ever since I've been looking for that same high and have gone through many a game only to be left disappointed. In steps Darkest Dungeon and suddenly I'm right back there. Don't get me wrong the Gameplay loop is very different but the stress and the thinking I have to employ to pass areas is very similar. I can honestly find myself getting addicted. Though they aren't real I find myself assigning personalities and character arcs to the people I play as, and I feel legit destroyed when one of my favs dies, because it's nearly always my fault. On god if Dismas dies at this point I'm going to have a mental breakdown. I did have some issues with frame drops and crashing but that pretty much cleared up upon changing the version when starting up. I know there's a sequel out there and maybe I'll try it but for now this is just a really solid yet challenging game.

Surprisingly, I had a lot of fun with the game. I wasn't a huge fan of BL1 and BL2 - both were kinda mid in my mind. I remember there being a huge hate bandwagon about the 2 main villains on release - and yeah, the dialogue and writing in this game is mostly bad, cringy and unfunny, with a decent amount of gross out "humor" to boot. But the gameplay and gunplay really do carry this game, with visuals (despite the ugly cel shading) and audio also being pretty good, and they all are better here than the previous two games by a wide margin. The guns, loot and gameplay Undeniably the best part. Yeah, it starts slow with guns that have poor accuracy, like in previous games, but it picks up fast and by the second half I was drowning in legendries, so much so that I was wiping most bosses, including the final story boss, in under a minute, just because I happened to kill an optional animal mini-boss on the way there. I did like the new feature of guns having alternative firing modes. Most of the time its something boring - a burst/auto switch, but for some guns they have cool gimmicks like the underbarrel grenade launcher or a shotgun, elemental type switch, auto aim puck, etc., depending on the gun manufacturer. The guns are kinda weird though. Most pistols seem to just be SMGs. This makes the SMG archetype pointless. Rocket Launchers also appear to be extremely underwhelming, at least in my playthrough and build, they did no more damage that regular guns, and had extremely poor ammo economy and slow firing speed, making them useless in my view. Then there are the weapon manufacturers. At least half of them have weird gimmicks - slow charge up times, throw-away reloads, overheat mechanics, slow projectiles, etc. What this all culminates in is that I stuck with like 3 "boring" manufactures, and mostly pistols and assault rifles, because that's what was most effective. The other 6 manufacturers and 4 gun archetypes were just immediately trashed, because they are either too weak or too annoying to use. Why would I use a cool looking gun that takes 10 shots to kill an enemy when I can use a boring gun that does it in 1? This becomes even more of a pain point on post-game Mayhem mode - where enemies can insta-snipe you from far way, making any non hitscan guns just non viable. The loot drops are also not really all that exciting when you realize, like with most games that have loot systems and leveling - all your guns WILL become obsolete. This works great to force the player to try new stuff, but makes loot less exciting. Yeah, I got a strong legendary. Maybe it looks a bit different from a normal gun. It will be useless in 10 levels. UI was kinda annoying, it seems to run at 20-30 FPS at all times regardless of your game performance, bugs out sometimes, and multiple times I crashed when in my inventory. They finally added a very hidden switch to turn off mouse steering for vehicles - and vehicles now have more upgrades which is cool. Other dislikes: * Online server BS * Some exploration stuff is hard locked behind main story progression with no indication of when you might unlock it. One of the collectibles can only be accessed after beating pretty much the whole main story. This really did disincentive exploration for me, and therefore doing all the side quests as well. Story It's not all bad. But it's kinda bad. Especially the dialogue writing. There are so many unfunny jokes as well as cringe and groan inducing dialogue, and there's a lot of dialogue in general, so much so that it is a common occurrence of voice overs overlapping or canceling each other out, especially when collectibles are involved. The overall story is not THAT bad, it's typical borderlands - bad guys, vaults. Some decent side quests here and there. References to other games and stuff that are actually entertaining.

**A Fantastic Open-World Zombie Game with Tons of Fun!** Dying Light 2 genuinely surprised me in a positive way. The parkour system is especially enjoyable. Running through the city, jumping across rooftops, and dodging zombies just feels incredibly satisfying. The combat system is also impressive. Melee fights are brutal, the weapons offer plenty of variety, and combining parkour with combat creates some truly awesome moments. Things get even more intense at night, when the atmosphere becomes much more threatening and every mistake can have serious consequences. The open world offers plenty to explore, tons of side quests, and many ways to develop and improve your character. Visually, the game also looks fantastic. Of course, not everything is perfect. The story could have been better in certain areas, and some activities become repetitive over time. However, for me, the overall enjoyment of the game easily outweighs these flaws. **Final Verdict:** If you enjoy zombies, open-world exploration, and action-packed combat, Dying Light 2 is definitely worth playing. It's a game you can easily sink countless hours into. The combination of freedom of movement, atmosphere, and survival elements is what makes Dying Light 2 stand out. **My Rating: 9/10 – Highly Recommended!**

This is frankly an incredible video game. It's a strong contender for my favorite game of all time. I always find myself coming back to it, year after year, while that isn't really the case with other games in the genre like minecraft or vintage story. There's something inherently extremely satisfying and immersive about the gameplay loop of surviving on some alien planet or in deep space, building or stealing a ship, and then losing it in a hail of gunfire somewhere along the way. I think it does something really unique amongst games in its genre, which is give you a reason to build things. There's genuine challenges to overcome, be they self made, part of a scenerio, or part of the vanilla "progression" with the factorum and such. And those challenges carry risks. You'll spend a lot of time building some rover or spaceship, and it's entirely possible something will go very wrong and it will end up a cloud of debris, forcing you to try again. Maybe you'll design a boarding pod to try to capture a ship, and have it fail over and over, making you rethink it and iterate on it until it works. It feels like there's always something to do even after you have your production set up. It's fun, and unique. Maybe you just feel like building something cool in creative, and you can absolutely do that too. The game is flawed of course. The physics are janky. It starts to lag if you build anything too big or fancy, butting up against the infamous "pcu limit". There's no npcs without mods, so you feel alone in a world of derelicts unless you play with friends. Multiplayer suffers streaming and desync issues. And worst of all, keen software house is... not a great developer and only cares about releasing an endless tide of DLC packs for the game, which might be the only game they haven't abandoned. The stuff in the DLCs isn't bad but the fact they exist at all while there's longstanding bugs going back a decade feels pretty scummy. That said I think they really caught lightning in a bottle with this game because it is a ton of fun and just, hits right despite its flaws. I very very highly recommend it. As for the dlcs? Wait for a sale. The mods? Absolutely fantastic. Go wild. Don't touch space engineers 2 with a 10 foot pole though.

Recommend if you care about gameplay, especially parkour and combat. I enjoyed both. Puzzles with capturing different structures weren't bad, but could be more varied. Most side quests are pretty generic and repetitive with nothing interesting to them outside of like two or three that actually had a pretty good story behind it. Do not recommend if you care about the main story, which is a disaster. Most characters are insufferable (aside from maybe two) and make little sense in terms of their actions half the time. I kind of liked the way you are supposed to choose between the two factions but only very little of it had any larger impact story wise. That being said, I very much enjoyed that visually and functionally the city transformed based on your actions. Opening up the map and creating safe zones was one of the most enjoyable parts of the game. With the severe cuts done to the prologue, some characters appear out of nowhere with no emotional impact. Aiden's main motivation is incredibly weak, especially since all you hear from Mia for most of the game is her yelling "Aiden babeiden" which just makes me want to kill her. Some of the main story scenes and characters will make you want to slam your head into the wall if you care about the narrative at all. Thankfully, the story is a small part of the game and the gameplay does make up for it in my eyes. I care about the story and the characters if they're good, if not, I can usually suffer through it for the sake of a good gameplay, so overall, I had a good time playing. Especially if I choose to believe that the entire last part was a fever dream. The game puts you back before those events anyway, if you want to keep playing, so it doesn't even matter.

I came in as someone who's been only a "casual" ARPG player. I'm a woman in my 40s, and I've been gaming ever since I got the NES I begged for Christmas in 1990. When I was in my 30s, literally 90% of my gaming focused on JRPGs. But in the past few years, I've reduced JRPGs to about 10-15% of my "gaming diet," with a lot more genre variety, including games that aren't RPGs at all. I probably played OG Diablo and Diablo II a bit as a teenager. Earlier this year, I sunk some hours into Grim Dawn, tried some other ARPGs, and I've now got an original EXE of Diablo II: Lord of Destruction running in Wine outside of Steam, on my Linux desktop. I know n00bs are usally scared away from PoE due to the immense skill... not a tree, more like a series of skill forests. I followed some of the advice from PoE YouTubers, I got a loot filter right away and I started following a build guide for a melee attack optimized Scion. But after allocating several points, I realized that the build guide didn't quite align with the skill "forest" I had. I did spend the first several points on upgrading my strength. And now at level 32, I have a few nice attack traits, such as impale anf bleed. Now that I'm navigating the skill "forest" with a lot more confidence, seeing patterns in how it's laid out while following the general advice to specialize rather than try to make my Scion a "Jill of all trades." I'm having a lot of fun. I'm glad the Trials of Ascendancy aren't complicated puzzles, The puzzles in CrossCode were bad enough, I don't want them in my more Diablo like ARPGs. I'm still not sure how to be more active in my league other than to check the events board (empty for now), and play those sea maps for Valerie. When I know other players can see my character, I will likely buy a few cosmetics. It took some fiddling to get the game to run well even though this is a mid tier gaming laptop from 2021. It's almost certainly because I'm running a version of Gentoo Linux, something I do because I'm a cybersecurity specialist and anti Gen AI political activist. If you have any sort of Linux distro, I strongly recommend going to ProtonDB before you launch the game for the first time and choose the version of Proton, and best launcher settings for your distro. Then, while in the game settings, switch networking (under the game tab) to either auto or predictive, never lockstep. I think I found predictive to be best. Even though my network connectivity is steady and fast, lockstep tends to lock me on the loading screen. Once I had the right version of Proton and launcher settings (including "no logo"?), and tweaked the in-game settings a bit, with my loot filter from filterblade dot xyz manually added (adding from the filterblade web app didn't work for me, search DuckDuckGo for "Path of Exile Linux loot filter location" if you need to know where to put it in your Linux PC's file system), the game has been running great, with loading screens not lasting more than a couple of seconds and always 60 FPS or more. I really appreciate how Chris Wilson and the rest of GGG appear to be very pro-consumer and have no interest in Gen AI or any of that horrifying crap. To n00bs, don't be afraid of the skill "forest." Zoom in and out of it, and make note of the patterns of skills in it. Also keep in mind that the kind of attack or magic skills that would consume MP in a JRPG usually come from gems. Make sure to put gems in your equipment ASAP! And keep most of the same gems through the campaign and end game, because they get more powerful and level up as you use them more.

text_clean: 时隔二十余年，《帝国时代 2：决定版》把无数玩家记忆里的经典 RTS 重新带回桌面。在 Steam 上保持着**特别好评**，它不是简单的高清换皮，而是在完整保留原版灵魂的基础上，完成了一次现代化重制。如果你是老玩家，这是重温青春最好的载体；如果你是新玩家，这是体验传统即时战略的教科书。 本作最大的亮点，就是原汁原味的核心玩法丝毫未变。黑暗时代、封建时代、城堡时代、帝王时代的升级节奏，采集资源、发展经济、扩张版图、集结军队的循环，依旧有着无与伦比的魅力。钟声一响，村民躲进城镇中心，这种刻在老玩家骨子里的紧张感完整保留。游戏内置数十个文明，每个文明拥有独特的单位、科技与加成，蒙古擅长骑射突袭、法兰克骑兵强势、不列颠长弓手远近闻名。不同文明的打法差异巨大，无论是防守运营还是快攻骚扰，都能找到适合自己的思路，重复游玩性极强。 画面上，决定版升级到 4K 高清画质，建筑、单位、地形全部重新绘制，光影、水面、植被细节大幅提升，同时保留原版美术风格，不会产生违和感。配乐也进行重录，熟悉的 BGM 经过重新编曲，氛围感拉满。战役内容极其丰富，从成吉思汗、圣女贞德到帖木儿，大量历史战役关卡，讲述不同文明的兴衰故事，新增的合作战役更是一大惊喜，可以和好友并肩完成历史剧本。内置场景编辑器与完整 MOD 支持，社区玩家自制的海量地图、战役、模组极大拓展游戏内容，让游戏的上限远高于本体。 但经典的底子，也带来一些无法回避的老问题。作为古早 RTS 的重制版，单位寻路依旧偶有拉胯，大量部队移动时容易出现卡堆、绕路的情况，在激烈对战中很容易影响战局。联机方面，服务器偶尔不稳定，匹配、掉线问题长期被玩家诟病；天梯环境里，炸鱼、消极游戏的情况时有发生，对新手不太友好。部分 DLC 内容质量参差不齐，新增文明与战役的口碑褒贬不一。操作逻辑源于老游戏，UI 设计偏传统，上手门槛偏高，新手很容易顾此失彼，一边管不住村民，一边被对手偷袭，需要大量对局练习才能入门。 它并不适合追求爽快、轻量化游戏的玩家。帝国时代 2 讲究经济运营、资源分配、侦查博弈，一场对局动辄几十分钟，需要耐心和专注力。但如果你愿意沉下心学习，会感受到 RTS 独有的成就感：从寥寥几个村民，一步步建立繁华城镇，组建大军击溃对手。 总而言之，《帝国时代 2：决定版》是 RTS 活化石。它带着老游戏固有的缺陷，却拥有难以替代的策略深度。老玩家可以回来重温情怀，新玩家如果想感受正统即时战略的魅力，它值得入手。有好友一起联机打战役、打对抗，体验会再上一个台阶。只要你能接受它古老机制带来的瑕疵，这便是一款可以玩上千小时的策略佳作。

game_name: The Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim Special Edition
text_clean: 时至今日，当众多新作追逐华丽画面与强引导叙事，《上古卷轴 5：天际》依旧是奇幻 RPG 不可逾越的丰碑。这片风雪笼罩的天际省，并非简单的游戏地图，而是一个呼吸着的诺德史诗世界。雪山与古冢、城镇与荒野之间，巨龙的咆哮回荡群山，古老的预言与内战纠葛交织。 它最伟大之处，在于给予玩家全然的自由。你不必被迫成为英雄，可做莽夫、法师、盗贼，循着自己的意志漫游。卷帙浩繁的典籍、鲜活的众生，构筑起厚重的泰姆瑞尔传说。即便岁月流逝，依托庞大 MOD 社群，天际仍生生不息。这是一部可供亲身踏入的奇幻史诗，所有热爱欧美 RPG 之人，都应当造访这片风雪大地。龙裔的宿命悬于头顶，你却可以搁置屠龙大业，流连于白漫城的酒馆，听吟游诗人传唱古老歌谣；或是深入地下古墓，探寻诺德亡灵守护的秘密。这片土地里的每一个小人物都承载着细碎故事，农夫的争执、流亡者的求助、黑夜里盗贼的密谋，交织成主线之外鲜活的人间。泰姆瑞尔大陆漫长的历史藏在遍布全省的书本与遗迹之中。翻开发黄的书卷，便能窥见湮灭危机、龙战争的遥远过往，厚重的奇幻设定并非空洞的背景板，而是沉淀在山川遗迹里的真实。行走在群山之间，风穿过松涛，远处隐约传来龙吼，这种沉浸式的旷野体验，时至今日依旧动人。 以当下标准审视，重置版的画面、动作系统难免陈旧，地牢设计也偶有重复。但这些表层缺陷，无法撼动其灵魂。MOD 社群长久的耕耘，不断翻新视觉效果、扩充故事，让天际跨越时代。《上古卷轴 5》的伟大，是它守住了老式欧美 RPG 最珍贵的内核：冒险不是完成任务清单，而是一段独属于你的旅途与选择。 2026了，风雪长存，龙鸣仍犹在，这片北国大地永远等候冒险者前来，没有什么唯一正确的故事走向，只有你写下的经历，才是天际真正的传奇。

The other benchmark. FTL and this one are the two games I hold every roguelike up against, and most of what comes out does not make it. People call this a deckbuilder and it is, but I think that undersells it. It is a decision game. The cards are just how the decisions show up. What Slay the Spire understands, and what most of its imitators never do, is that every card you take is a bet on where the run is going. Not a bonus. A bet. Take the big attack and you are committing to a deck that wants to end fights fast and you had better find the draw to support it. Skip it and you are saying you trust the defense you have not found yet. Fifteen floors later, that one pick is the reason you won or the reason you are staring at the heart with no answer, and here is the part that matters. The game is clear enough that you always know which pick it was. You never lose to something you could not have seen. You lose because you made a bet and it did not come in, and you can trace the line back to the exact floor where you made it. That clarity is rare. It is the whole reason the game is replayable, because every loss is a lesson instead of an excuse. The other thing it gets right is that nothing in it is wasted. Every character is a different game with the same rules. Ironclad plays like a brawl, Silent plays like a trap, Defect plays like an engine, Watcher plays like you are holding a loaded gun the entire fight. The relic system means that even two runs with the same deck plan feel completely different, because the relics are what change the math. And the ascension ladder is the best difficulty system I have seen in anything. It does not make enemies spongier. It takes things away from you, one at a time, until the run you used to cruise through becomes a real fight again. There is always a next ascension and there is always a reason to go for it. There is no story to speak of and it does not need one. The run is the story. You remember the run where you found the one relic that turned a dead deck into a monster. You remember the run where you had the heart at ten health and drew the wrong card. Those are the stories and they are better than most games manage with a script. Honest criticism. The art is functional and that is being generous. The game is a decade old and it looks it. And if you do not like thinking three turns ahead you will not like this, because that is the entire game and there is no mode that lets you skip it. I own the sequel now and I have been putting real hours into it. But when someone asks me where to start with roguelikes, this is still the first thing I say, because everything that came after is standing on it. Shout out to Mega Crit.

Black Myth: Wukong My Journey to the West — 130+ Hours Later I had not anticipated that the game would take more than 130 hours. And yet, I find myself approaching the conclusion of my personal "Journey to the West." I took a methodical approach, exploring at my own pace and occasionally optimising my equipment more than was necessary. I was pleasantly surprised by the extensive range of content available. Each chapter unveils new features and storylines, consistently maintaining my interest. I was rarely bored, and best of all, I was so immersed in the activity that I did not notice the time passing. Indeed, I am still playing to increase the difficulty with highly optimised gear. Gameplay, Combat & Progression In terms of gameplay, I found the difficulty level to be fairly balanced for a first playthrough. However, the difficulty level of some bosses was notably higher than others. I particularly appreciated the variety of skills and upgrades, which allowed for customisation of combat styles. Depending on the boss, certain stances proved more effective than others to vary their approach rather than sticking to a single strategy. The game offers a wide range of weapons that prioritise power or critical hits, as well as skills that can be developed. In addition, there are armour sets that combine to offer additional bonuses, allowing plenty of room to experiment and fine-tune your setup. The healing system is well-designed, with various flasks to unlock and drinks to combine for bonus effects. The bestiary is also impressive, featuring creatures and bosses with meticulous designs. The weapons and armour are impressive, and each discovery stimulates the desire to explore new possibilities. I would also like to express my appreciation of the ability to reset my skills at will, thus allowing me to experiment with different combat styles. Furthermore, I would have appreciated greater flexibility in the use of armour upgrade resources. In my personal experience, I have sometimes held back on certain items due to concerns about wasting them on equipment that I was planning to replace. This has sometimes resulted in missing out on potentially beneficial upgrades. Visuals, Art Direction & Sound Visually, I was extremely impressed. The settings in the various chapters are stunning, but it is the animation, the creatures' movements, and the visual effects that truly set this production apart. The art direction is a complete success. Even the animated sequences are charming and well-executed. The music skilfully transitions from a supporting role to a more prominent one during the most intense scenes. The key benefit of this approach is that it does not rely on visual cues or secondary characters to guide the user. However, it should be noted that there are some aspects that could be improved. The most significant issue I have encountered is the presence of invisible walls, which can be frustrating when attempting to navigate detailed environments. Story & Lore — A Journey Worth Knowing In terms of the storyline, Black Myth: Wukong is set in a highly detailed universe, although the narrative world is not always clearly explained. The game draws inspiration from the famous Chinese novel Journey to the West, which recounts the journey of the monk Xuanzang to India, accompanied by the iconic Monkey King, Sun Wukong. This character is renowned for his cunning, his power, and his ability to shapeshift, making him an iconic figure in Chinese mythology. In addition, he was the source of inspiration for the character Son Goku in the well-known manga Dragon Ball. I found the references to Chinese mythology to be of great interest. However, it should be noted that without prior knowledge of the subject, certain events may appear confusing and difficult to understand. At times, I would have preferred the storytelling to be more immersive, so as to better grasp the story's stakes. The animated sequences are of a high standard and significantly enhance the overall appeal of the adventure. Conclusion — Worth the Wait After such a long anticipation for this game, it was only natural to have some reservations, as is often the case when expectations are set too high. However, I was incorrect. Black Myth: Wukong met my expectations and even exceeded them thanks to the richness of its content. Despite a few minor issues, these are outweighed by the significant enjoyment derived from extensive gameplay. I therefore have no hesitation in recommending it. The memorable combat, the exceptional bestiary, the sublime art direction, and an adventure that lasted much longer than expected all contributed to making this game a worthwhile purchase. Following 130 hours of gameplay, my sole objective is to reconnect with my team members and commence the adventure once more. Finally, it appears that the Monkey King has gained a valuable life lesson: material wealth is not necessarily a prerequisite for happiness. In contrast, the key elements of happiness are a capable team and the ability to overcome challenges. If you are having difficulty following the narrative, there is no cause for concern. Simply read Journey to the West, or acknowledge that the intricacies of Son Goku's tale exceeded initial expectations.

Pros: * The core gameplay is great. You kill huge hordes of monsters. * The skill gem system is cool. You can build your own skill. * Mapping is arguably the best end game system in gaming. * It's free! Cons: * Too many one-shot mechanics. * The boss design is often very poor. You must learn the boss mechanics by heart, and the game doesn't teach you those mechanics. * It is extremely imbalanced. It's not "anything goes". There are only a few "good" builds. * Off-screening. * There is grinding. * Maps have become bloated with content you don't want to interact with. * Playing standard is miserable because your build often gets nerfed and becomes obsolete. You must play league, which means you must constantly start over. Some people enjoy that. I don't enjoy it because it takes many hours (estimately at least 40) to get a character to the endgame. * The campaign is not enjoyable. It's boring. * There is no multiplayer. It is a single player game where you can trade with other players who also play single player. * Melee builds are much worse than ranged. The clear speed is too low. * Every monster in the game has stun on hit. * In spite of much cool content, the addition of the "atlas tree" made it meaningless to interact with most of the content because it became too unrewarding. I almost only played standard (the permanent league where you never start over). I got tired of the nerfs. The final straw for me was when they changed the rules for socket colors. Players in standard had perfect items with 6 white sockets, which required tons of investment. Then the developers suddenly reversed it and said that white sockets are now strictly worse. It felt like an insult. All my items became worse and I can't fix them because they are mirrored. I recommend the game for its good parts, but you must play league, not standard. This may not be the best dungeon crawler, best roguelike, or best turn based games I've played. However, this game has one of the best themes, and it sticks to it like glue. The story, albeit simple, glued me to this game for my first 5-10 hours. I now play it an hour a day, do a few runs, and move on. This game respects your time thats for sure. Its hard, sometimes hair pulling hard, but not the hardest. There is plenty of room to learn mechanics, counters, so on. The game has flaws, all games do, but this game is just so catching. Its one of my favourites, its soundtrack is godly, and its atmosphere is second to none. (also a good avenue into lovecraftian lore/horror) The opening has lived rent free in my brain since I first seen it, and I unironically make quotes of the narrator when playing other games. Maybe do what I do and have this as a "secondary playthrough" game, where you take breaks from your main games to chip away a few dungeon runs into this one, I promise you the change of pace is a great palate cleanser. That's specially the case if you are starting to feel burnt out of the potential grind, or just feel the need to take a break, Its very likely unique enough from whatever you are playing beside it. All in all I think this game is amazing, I do not much care for its DLCs, most have been not the best: I either dislike them or have no opinion on them. But this game, Darkest Dungeon, is amazing and worth the try. Either as your new game to be hooked on, or a new side hustle to chip away while you grind other games, either way its a great time.

I love this game, I really do, but no matter how much love I pour into it, it does not make it any less broken. The beginning of the game is excellent: nice, steady progression, good challenge, gradual level ups. The transition from apprentice to veteran is tough but surmountable, and I was having a great time. And then you hit champion level. The characters levels cap at 6, along with their armor and attack capabilities, and if the monsters in the new area were just harder hitting and had more effects with their attacks, that would be fine. Instead, the balance is utterly ruined by massively buffing their dodge and crit rate. The game changes completely from a challenging but fair experience that requires planning, forethought, and skill, and turns into a lottery roll. You go into champion dungeons just crossing your fingers that you don't run into monsters with attacks that crit nearly every time, attacks that can and will OHKO multiple party members in one swing, and so on. And these are NOT bosses. These are random enemy encounters where a 75% chance to hit equates to missing five times in a row, then having the enemy critical hit multiple characters in one turn and deathblow them before you can even blink. Now I know there are people out there that love this, and I'm glad there are because everyone deserves a game that hits just right for them. Unfairness is a genuine appeal to some players, and that's okay, but if that is not something that appeals to you, don't play this game. Don't sink hours into it only to get two thirds of the way in and be completely stonewalled by RNG. I'm sure a lot of people would laugh at this review and say "if you don't like challenge, then this isn't the game for you" but in my opinion, challenge and RNG are complete opposites. Challenge is something that requires skill to overcome. There is no way to overcome RNG. There is no combat tactic that will stop a crit sweep. There is no prior planning that can mitigate losing your vital trinkets that you cannot ever get back. That's not challenge, and it's not fun for me. If I wanted to play an RNG game that I will always lose, I'd buy a lottery ticket. As for DD, I think I need to just uninstall it. At least I had some fun before it shot itself in the foot.

和朋友联机玩了挺久，先说结论：单人能玩，多人一坨。 联机bug是真的一堆，还都不是小毛病。最典型的是坐电梯：电梯还在底下，人已经跑到电梯上面卡死了，在里面怎么走都出不来，只能让朋友拉过去传送，或者干脆退游戏重进。这不是偶发，基本上每次坐电梯都能撞上。 画面这块大问题没有，主要就是光影有一点点毛病。 最难受的是更新之后剧情被删了一大截。我和朋友联机打到后面，连结局的CG都没了，就这么没了！！！！！！！！！ 道具系统也是折磨，一堆东西全得靠肝，任务又臭又长，点名贾伊，肝到怀疑人生。 剧情里的NPC一个比一个蠢，离了主角连路都不会走，这毛病跟一代一模一样。 十分我能给六七分，这六七分还是看在跑酷和画面上给的。 这游戏停止更新是好事，终于不用再被霍霍了， （这是我本人的主观评测，如果你觉得不顺眼，点个踩就行了） 好了，说说这游戏的优点，这游戏创意还行，然后也有那种打击的爽感，音乐也是蛮好听的，但是跟一代的神作相比，差距还是蛮大的。 如果你是想史底入坑的话，直接入也还算可以，不亏，毕竟这玩意也蛮有意思的，那种晚上的紧张氛围感也十分的充足，就是这游戏真的有点像育碧的那种罐头游戏。 总的来说，这游戏史低入坑不亏，如果想体验那种跑酷，还有晚上躲夜魔的那种紧张氛围感的话，也还算可以，但是剧情的话就不用太指望了。

A brilliant, oceanic survival sandbox that transforms a stranded-at-sea nightmare into a deeply addictive and cozy crafting experience. You start on a tiny 2x2 wooden square armed only with a plastic hook, and your goal is to pull trash from the ocean to build a massive, floating fortress. The progression loop is incredibly rewarding as you transition from basic survival to automation and island exploration, though the repetitive early-game gathering and the relentless, annoying shark can test your patience. PROS: • Incredibly satisfying base-building that lets you build massive, fully customized rafts. • Addictive progression loop from basic plastic-hooking to high-tech automation. • Smooth and deeply engaging co-op experience—perfect to play with friends. • Exploring unique, story-driven islands adds a refreshing break from drifting. CONS: • Early-game resource gathering can feel highly repetitive and slow. • The shark mechanic is less scary and more of a constant, annoying chore.

It Takes Two — Couple's Therapy, With Unnecessary Elephant Trauma I'll admit it: I started It Takes Two sceptical. My usual taste leans towards gritty, realistic, and often brutal games like GTA V, Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order and Survivor, and Detroit: Become Human. So, naturally, this colourful, cartoonish adventure looked like a bit of a departure from my usual gaming diet. But this was the first co-op game I played with my fiancée, and I'm SO glad I gave it a chance. THE STORY — MORE THAN JUST A CUTE LITTLE ADVENTURE Beneath its colourful art style lies a genuinely heartfelt story about a relationship that's been falling apart for years. It explores love, frustration, resentment, and the difficult process of finding your way back to someone. What really stood out to both of us was the ending. It doesn't magically fix years of broken trust and accumulated problems just because two people spend a few hours working together. But it shows that those hours can be a beginning. A first step towards something better. And honestly? That hit harder than I expected from a game featuring talking household objects. THE GAMEPLAY — TWO BRAINCELLS, ONE OBJECTIVE The gameplay is an absolute blast. Every level introduces new mechanics, abilities, and challenges that constantly change how you and your partner need to cooperate. Just when you've mastered one set of mechanics, the game throws something completely different at you. Communication matters, teamwork matters, and sometimes you will absolutely blame your partner for your own spectacular failure. It's practically relationship counselling with platforming. And that upside-down section? No spoilers, but we had a great time with that one. THE ELEPHANT — I WANT A LAWYER If you've played it, you know. If you haven't, I'm not spoiling it. All I'll say is that I went into this game expecting a wholesome co-op adventure, and I came out carrying emotional damage caused by an elephant. THE VERDICT It Takes Two surprised me in the best possible way. The story is heartfelt, the gameplay constantly stays fresh, and sharing the experience with my fiancée made it all the more special. You don't need to be a fan of colourful platformers. You don't even need to think this is your kind of game. Just find someone you love, grab a second controller, and give it a chance. 9/10. One point deducted for the elephant incident. I will never financially or emotionally recover.

I loved it at the beginning, but the more I progress the more boring it gets. You have magic abilities that do a huge amount of damage, but these have a long cooldown. They can also be interrupted, restaring the cooldown. For some bosses, doing melee attacks is almost useless so you basically run around waiting for the cooldowns to end. Some bosses have incredibly long combos that kill you off if you do not evade most of the attacks, and the drawn-out feeling of the boss fights makes learning them a chore. You also frequently fight the camera, not only because sometimes you simply don't see anything if you stand near a wall or a tree, but also because it is very difficult to actually estimate the range of your charged melee attacks, so you charge up an attack only to have it end an inch in front of the boss. Bosses sometimes have a weakness or you can equip some item to make the fight a bit easier, but in many cases this is very obscure. Due to all this, beating a difficult boss did never feel like "yeah I earned this" but more often like "o.k., I was lucky this time." Yes, the world-building is nice, if you know "Journey to the West" you'll recognize several things, graphics is also godd to very good, but if gameplay is not fun, none of these can save a souls-like.

(This review contains minor mechanical spoilers, and mentions minor details about the sequel at the end) Hades is one of the few games I always enjoy returning to, even after having completed the full story several times. The incredible attention to detail and unique style present in every aspect of the game have always impressed me, from the first time I played. The story is extremely well-written, immersive, and impactful. I was hooked to it and eager to progress it all the way through, and have started up a new save file to experience it again several times over the years. Progress feels meaningful and personal. More than any other game I have played, the world feels developed and alive. Characters have depth and respond to the things the player does, sometimes in the funniest and most unexpected ways. After over 200 hours of gameplay, I still encounter dialogues I haven't seen before. I greatly enjoy the combat system. It's simple but also has a high ceiling to develop your skill, and there is lots of room for personal preference. There are many mechanics which exist to provide variety to the builds you can make and incentives for exploring that variety, but also freedom to play the way you want to. There is room to choose how difficult you want the game to be— whether more casual to experience the story, or more challenging to push your limits. Players who enjoy challenges can utilize some optional mechanics that increase the difficulty in creative ways which push you to make use of everything you can, and be rewarded for doing so. Unlike many games, it's not just artificial difficulty either, there is genuinely unique content to enjoy in doing so (i.e. not just numbers going up, which is part of it, but also interesting twists and enemies gaining new attacks & abilities). There is also SO much content and replayability. Outside of the main story, there are so many other things you can choose to explore and progress, including side storylines, customizations, challenges, additional worldbuilding, and more. It doesn't feel like a chore, either— you can work on many things at once by just playing the game. Completionists can have a field day trying to max everything out if they so please. And, since the dungeons are randomized and there are so many build choices, no two runs feel the same. You are compelled to improve your adaptability and be ready for anything. At the same time, I would say the RNG is well-balanced, and there are systems you can unlock to greatly mitigate build-based RNG once you start finding ones you like to go for. Overall, I would say Hades deserves all the awards and nominations it's received and more, and I can easily recommend it to a variety of players. You can tell the developers put the utmost of their efforts and passion into making it. I love the art style and original music so much I've used screenshots as my desktop background and listen to the music outside of the game. With Hades 2 out now, there's even more to look forward to afterwards. I would highly recommend playing the original first, as while Hades 2 has its own story, it builds on the story from the first game and has lots of fun references.

Borderlands 3, truth be told I really enjoy this game. The looting, shooting, traversal, level design, enemy design, sound design and soundtrack. Pretty much everything to do with the core gameplay is fantastic. The drop rates and selection for items I personally think is the best of all the BL games, it tows that line of, you will get legendaries to drop a lot but whether you get good parts rolls determines the viability of them which I greatly enjoy and tickles the loot goblin in me. The Gunplay is still the slight edge of wackyness and realism that previous titles brought, and each vault hunter is viable and has very fun unique action skills. Swapping between those action skills and crafting builds I think is the strongest here over the previous games. Now the story, is all over the place for me. The main campaign storyline is definitely the weakest its ever been, but there are still many many likable characters (along with a few unlikeable) that are still written decent for what they're trying to be. The DLCs are where they definitely improved greatly on the story telling, and actually impressed me with how much better the writting for the DLCs is. In short, Its a very fun game to play, don't get too attached to the story/characters, blast psyco's in the dome and get Shlootin!

If you were looking for a raft-building survival crafting game that takes place on the water, this is the one to go to! I think your alternatives are Tidewrack (not as well rated) or Stranded Deep (not raft-focused). It's fun, but there are some frustrations. Quite a number of tools are a mystery to unlock and use. In particular, I spent about 50 hours of the game just doing base building -- having fun, mind you -- before I realized I hadn't "researched" copper, which ludicrously unlocks circuit boards, then antennas, then radar and ... GPS mapping systems??? Until then you'll simply hit the same islands over and over and will never locate any of the storyline. And the storyline? Well it's fine. It's uneven. The story is about people who came before you, what happened to the world such that it's all so wet all over, and the struggles they dealt with. A lot of the tech tree is silly, just go in knowing that and you'll be fine. This is not ultrarealism. There is a meager list of nice-to-have items that make raft travel better but most are unlocked well into the story. For me I was already done at that point having put in nearly 100 hours. Some of that time was spent getting back up to speed: every time you die, you lose 2/3rds of your stuff. If you're playing multiplayer, apparently, you can be resuscitated by a friend, and keep your stuff, but if you're single player shame on you. There's no body you can fetch, you just lose most of your stuff, so make sure to leave unnecessary crap in a locker before you do a dangerous thing. Also quick tip don't do any renovating near your lockers or chests, because you may accidentally trigger a timespace conniption whereby all your contents try to exist in the same space at the same time and you lose almost everything. That was fun. I didn't throw anything across the room at all, I was very poised. You use a scrap hook to pick up scrap metal off the ocean floor, but the shovel won't work. You use a machete to strike a shark or warthog, but not an axe. You melt iron ore into metal bars which is used to build most heavy things, but you get nails from scrap which can't be likewise melted down. You can't use a shovel to row your raft, because that needs a paddle, and a paddle requires plastic. Lots of little things like that. Still, you get to explore different islands, fight off sharks, build fairly big raft mobile homes if you want to invest the time, craft things into other things, and get an under-playtested but worthwhile back story. I had fun.

On release u couldnt climb infinitely since climbing was tied to stamina which made no sense since Aiden is superhuman due to experimentation. Also nights had no volatiles roaming on release which was fundamentally flawed. The survivors are so incredibly unlikeable, and most of the characters regardless of faction are unrelatable and two dimensional. Also combat feels limb and weak in comparison to DL1. They addressed this later thank god with some updates and patches but the launch left a bad taste. The plot is pretty boring, convoluted, and dragged out and choices have no real meaning expect for a couple which I wont spoil. And exploring was kinda dumbed down since it marked everything on the map if u used ur binoculars, and even then the GRE buildings and GRE anomalies were the only ones worth totally exploring. Don't even get me started on how repetitive the GRE buildings are. I tried to gaslight myself into liking this game (hence my hours) but I really couldn't even after the updates to fix it. In summary DL2 Feels soulless and like an artificial playground, there's even huge yellow markers on the buildings telling u where to go like typically AAA slop. In comparison DL1 while not being known for its story, its still widely remembered and has emotional depth. Dl1 had an amazing deeply interconnected map with environmental story telling, and a soundtrack amplifying the atmosphere. I was so incredibly disappointed on release dyling light 2 didn't match the quality they achieved in 2015. On the bright side the parkour is much better, human combat is actually fun, and there are more side quests than DL1 and a couple of them are really well written and have meaningful choices. Also the game is improving slowly its in a much better state now, most of my criticisms like easy night, limited climbing stamina, and combat have been fixed somewhat. I feel playing Dl1 and DLTB is much more worth ur while u aren't missing on much.

Fantastic game. I mean i could really just stop there, but i won't lol. This game has kept my attention every time i go to play it, usually each time i put in 50-100 hours just exploring and seeing what's new and to be honest... i still haven't done everything in the game. I would for sure recommend this game if you like base building, exploring and fun combat. Be warned, there is a BIT of a story in this, but it does NOT hold your hand. You have to find it all yourself. There are no markers or waypoints or magic lines to guide you (save the ones you put down). They give you clues and SOMETIMES a picture drawn so you can look for landmarks to help you find it. Even with all of that, you will get lost just exploring, making new "friends" and building awesome bases. Then when you get a base built you can do siege stuff. This is where you put a treasury down and npc enemies try to take your loot and that's just ONE of the endgame things. They are also dungeons, bosses and a whole other area to explore in Siptah. The co-op/multiplayer is also really fun. You are not tethered AT all to anyone else, so you could build a base on the far opposite side of the entire map with no problem and never see your friends again! (a bonus for some lol). That said, if you do decide to get this game, i hope you have a fantastic time with it, and thanks for reading! ~Mystikos

用心做手游，用脚做端游。你们当初做手游的那一天就应该会想到这个结果。 BUG不修、翻译问题也不改善，方舟IP的门面都这样，那些重制版和DLC一定很差。我只觉得是土上雕花、腐木地基上的危楼 它的生存元素特别少，它更像是《原神》和《宝可梦》的结合，不作死的前提下，每天吃点肉就能度过余生；遇到的任何敌人都能变成友方单位。 生物空有其表，没有智慧。连欺软怕硬的机制都没有。比如美颌龙，我骑迅猛龙它挑衅我，我骑着南巨它照样挑衅我 大部分生物快死了也不知道逃跑 恐龙遇到危险生物的反应不如其他游戏的护主犬，没有任何主动预警，仿佛在说，好开心，一会儿我们就去见上帝了 非常喜欢恶心玩家，比如蚂蚁和蜻蜓 恐龙被驯服完全是因为爱上了玩家，依据就是只有玩家在附近，恐龙才肯下蛋 陆地上走着走着，你能发现左脚的地方气温100℃，右脚的地方气温-100℃ 现在的方舟有以下BUG： 驯服的恐龙，自己记性差就永远找不到了。 驯服飞行恐龙时，天上没有太阳，但一抬头就莫名其妙的晃眼睛。 培养下一代恐龙时，如果默认设置里不调整，就永远不能留痕。 看地图时，毛皮套装和吉利套装直接穿模，地图的一部分直接被穿模覆盖。 飞行龙攻击大型生物时，打着打着大型生物就可能消失。

从一开场，滚5就展现了高超的制作水平。你和你操控的角色都是初到天际，对背景故事一无所知，在马车上的交谈中窥见世界的一角，在刑场登记信息时捏脸，在逃离龙的袭击时学会移动，在与帝国兵的冲突中学会基本的战斗操作，在地牢中搜刮物品学会和环境互动和开锁，在躲藏熊的时候学会潜行……直到逃出洞穴，看到远处覆雪的荒瀑古坟，一首《Far Horizons》响起，你完全自由了，在这个陌生的天际。没有给定的任务路线，没有空气墙和等级限制，“看见那座山了吗？你可以爬上去。” 经验值不来自杀敌，不来自完成任务，不来自白痴学者，玩家变强的路只有一条：你玩得多。滚5的等级来自于你所有熟练项的熟练度的总和，刀剑、魔法、锻造、炼金、附魔……所有技能的起点都是一样的，玩家不需要在一开始就决定存档里要当什么职业吃什么增益，你只需要多尝试自然就会了。当然也不排除一些技能设计失衡，譬如无脑强的钳工流和三神左脚踩右脚。一些技能的形同滚木，滚5的口才系统相比于辐射实属是一坨，除了能少花点钱和跳过一些重复劳动以外毫无用处，无法获得任何额外的重要信息；开锁技能树更是全程几乎零收益。再由于开场中没有法术教学，加之剧情中诺德人的文化旋律，本游戏的法术系统一直都有些被忽视，大部分玩家包括我除非被堵路或推剧情都鲜少使用魔法。但起码在原版内容里，法术的丰富程度要远胜于冷兵器，五大学派的法术设计都很完善，输出、奶、幻术或是摇人，玩法选择比只有我砍我再砍的近战武器好太多了。 任务设计，优秀夹杂着平庸。滚5有大量剧情优秀体验沉浸的任务线，主线、内战、战友团、工会、兄弟会、学院、龙裔和黎明守卫8条中除了内战战友团学院稍逊，其余几条甚至足以拿来单开一部3A游戏。除此还有大量游离在线外的优秀魔神任务和城市任务。但还是有两大缺点：1.依旧有不少通马桶，事实上滚5的马桶是无限制的，在你把地图杀光前无限刷新。而精品支线是有限的，且大部分都可以在第一次抵达相关城市获取，因此不难感受到玩得越久、马桶含量越高。2.任务分支平淡，绝大多数任务都是线性的，不像辐射和博德任务的错综，实话讲滚5还远远没有摸到网状叙事的门槛，剩下的一小部分也常常只是一个道德层面的二择。 不避讳地说，和互联网大多数人的观点一样，滚5原版的打击感确实是一坨大便，但处决动画还挺帅的。如果你作为资深老屁股不在意这些便无所谓，如果在意可以通过打Attack MCO-DXP来解决。 美学：19/20 天际，诺德，粗犷的北境。大地的绝大部分由白雪覆盖，冻岩冻土上永远飘荡着不死的冰雾，地势崎岖山峦耸立，天空绝大部分时间只雾蒙蒙，偶尔才能瞥见几眼太阳，让远处山的轮廓可见。星空，极光和两颗卫星之下，到处都是废弃的洞穴、古坟和矮人遗迹，被强盗和弃誓者盘踞，山花、浆果、草荚、松和其他枯树是主流的植被，远处时不时传来龙的吼叫。遍布薰衣草的白漫、四季如秋的裂谷、山岩拼接的马卡斯、偶然出现的巨大神像和湮灭领域风格迥异的建筑与装潢点缀这个冰冷的世界，天际的美术充满了灵魂。独自行走在其中，正如同本作11年11月11日的发售时间一般孤独。 叙事方面，许多任务线的叙事都相当优秀，保持了高度的戏剧冲突：玩家在黑暗兄弟会执行重大刺杀任务的同时不得不卷入组织内部的权力斗争、黎明守卫的推动就意味着和哈孔的对抗等；人物塑造也相当鲜明，瑟拉娜、帕图纳克斯、西塞罗等角色都令人印象深刻；但叙事节奏拉胯：全程站桩对话，NPC走路时而墨迹时而又不等人。环境本身也在叙事，一处强盗营地的信件、尸体和物品摆放，就可以让玩家推测这里发生了什么，一个疯乞丐的言语，就能透露村子尘封的历史，这些叙事不直接服务任务，却在细枝末节中透出世界的真实感。玩家也是一种叙事，你做过什么，城中的卫兵会对此夸赞或者讽刺，NPC会出现额外的对话选项。 上古卷轴的世界观是我见过最奇特的虚构世界观。在全天际中你能获得大量不同主题和类型的书籍，你会发现其中不同的种族对不同的神称呼、看法和历史记载均不一，模糊的历史为玩家提供了充分的想象空间和代入感。如同真实的世界一样，你不知道为什么遗迹会长成那样、为什么政治和宗教会在此冲突，但这确实发生了。这是一种相比碎片化叙事更高明的手法。 游戏哲学：10/10 想尽办法让玩家沉浸在游戏其中，这是Bethesda长期坚持的设计理念中的首要一件。沉浸感，一切夸赞上古卷轴5的文案都会提及的部分。在游戏中，玩家不再是一个扮演主角剧本的外世之人，我就是龙裔本身，我做的就是龙裔做的，龙裔的行为就是我的行为，在小小的屏幕中，二者完全达成了统一。不知多少次当我关闭exe，转头望向窗外微白的天空时，猛然意识到又回到了原来的世界，变成了一个其他的角色。 NPC的灵性绝对是讨论上古卷轴5时无法绕开的。每个城市中数十个有名有姓的NPC都有一套自己的行程表，日出而作日入而息、偶尔去一趟城里的神殿祈祷、或在酒店做些站场子的工作，熟悉的人相互遇到的时候也会交流打趣，即使没有玩家，天际省的时间依旧能自然流动下去。当然玩家对NPC造成的交互也同样生动，会问是吸血鬼或狼人的玩家身上的某些特征，玩家掏出武器和魔法时让玩家放下或走开，根据玩家不同的技能水平做出点评；玩家直接或间接造成NPC的死亡，他的家人可能会改变对你的态度和台词，甚至改变自己的工作。当你路过路边两个天天争吵的NPC并插了一次话后，可能就会开启一小时甚至几小时的一条支线任务。NPC在玩家的眼中变得更加重要，而不是一堆围着转的工具人。这是一个你不用只盯着头上冒出感叹号的NPC的游戏，NPC的设计正是上古卷轴5沉浸感的第一大来源。 十五年后回头来看，滚5的城市简直就是一个破村子，村子更是两栋烂房子拼成的怎么看都像在从事非法活动的不明聚集点。但这在我看来完全不是缺点，NPC可以密集聚居，方便他们之间的演出，游戏里的几乎每栋房子都有有名有姓的NPC可以交流触发任务推动剧情。嘴一下Bethesda，这种良好习惯自辐射4就不再有了，为了扩充地图那个byd新手村康科德就开始加入一堆无法进入的房屋，实属破坏体验。野外的兴趣地点也相当丰富，可以说滚5用着系列最小的地图容纳了系列最丰富的内容，许多地点可能同时有二到三条任务一同指向，一个任务又涉及两三个地点，清晰又庞大的任务网便这么展开了。游戏后期打开地图，看着立体的3D地图和上面密密麻麻承载故事的地点，充实感油然而生。地图设计的优秀是沉浸感的另一大来源。 所见即所得。滚5的所有生物都有着和玩家一视同仁的逻辑，背包里有什么就用什么穿什么，掉落物品不再是一坨预设好的序列，你看到一个强盗头头有发光的宝剑，杀了他或偷过来就能拿到，看到一个贵族有钻石制的项链，杀了他或偷过来就能拿到，不会有随机爆神级戒指的小龙虾、不用天天蹲在性价比高的野怪刷新点。一切杂物都有自己的独立建模，可以被随意摆在桌上扔在地上或扣在NPC的头上，更好的盾牌不是仅仅数值高一点，你可以在物品栏打开它，放大查看细节、雕纹，就和在NPC和你手上拿的时候一样。这是第三大来源。 完成度：8/15 Bug, bug never changes. 玩家会自己生产优化游戏的内容，这便是Bethesda所坚持的第二件。我的沉浸感不知多少次被Bug破坏得粉碎，九圣灵在上，不是所有bug都如同巨人航天一样有意思。 另外从不少代码和隐藏房间中可以看出，Bethesda自己也砍掉了不少有意思的支线，算是这个制作组的通病了。 内容量：10/10 十五年已过，天际依旧是社区活力最强规模最庞大的单机游戏。可能这个title不会改变，如果你在滚6发行之前不幸趋势了。我全成就用了190h。具体内容可见“游戏哲学”一栏。 但是聊上古卷轴不可避免的便是它的mod社区。Creation Engine这个引擎就拥有这么一个神奇的魔力，一切都可以自己修改。画质上跟不上时代了？我们有高清纹理mod、光影优化mod、光追路追mod、高模mod、天气系统mod，角色改进更是完全开出了一片新领域。战斗太无聊了？我们有动作系统mod、伤害系统mod，你可完全把它改装成ARPG。内容不够玩？我们有数不清的内容拓展mod，新任务、新地区、新的剧情NPC。细节不够精致？站桩对话修改mod、丰富婚姻系统mod、自由视角mod、UImod……而且，模组前置的机制可以让mod身上再长出mod，把你想要的继续客制化。不少优秀的任务mod会被官方转正成游戏内容，甚至一个新的二创游戏。这是一个由玩家作为创作者的平台，但bethesda的吃相实在是太sm了，差评中99%都是有关这点的。 创新性：9/10 第一个大满贯游戏，划时代的意义。把辐射3/新维加斯那种传统的桌游化的CRPG体系大幅改进，复杂的系统在新玩家眼中尽可能消失，但在老玩家眼中又不失深度，是一种相当适合电子游戏的设计理念。 黑箱：9/10 陶大炮，我再信你一次。

Note, that i will talk about prices here. This applies to regional pricing in many countries. This game is pretty cool for what it is and has plenty of interesting mechanics and content. It requires a lot of creativity and is very rewarding. However it is not nearly worth the amount of money developers ask for it. They have some very aggressive monetization tactics. Each and every update they add a new DLC which adds a couple of new textures/models for blocks which costs a lot more than it should. Imagine you bought a creative game like minecraft. You expect full creative freedom, a lot of building blocks and features and intead you get a pack of basic cobblestone and wood blocks, stairs and slabs and all other building blocks are locked behind paid DLCs which in their entirety cost ~4 times more than the base game. Yes, you can build a house with those and you still can play the game with all its technical features, but you don't have nearly enough creative freedom. Yes, developers swear that all "gameplay" features/mechanics are always available for free in the base game, it's true, but when your core gameplay is BUILDING STUFF, and you can't build nearly as much pretty stuff without all the skins and blocks DLCs provide - you get frustrated. Base game has only around 25-30% of visual blocks available without DLCs. I do not recommend buying this game. It's NOT worth the full price you'll have to pay for it and it's DLCs

I have played more than 25 hours of this game and still have lot of content left to discover. It is one of the best roguelite games of all time with crisp combat and funny parodies of other legendary 2D games like Hollow Knight, Katana Zero etc. Apart from the gorgeous pixel-art, the game has amazing soundtracks and the level design is one of the best I have seen in 2D games. No single run is same, you keep discovering new weapons, abilities etc. and the game has quite a few challenging bosses. The game is somewhat on the difficult side, though you keep unlocking stuff it does take time if you are not good with combat. I played the game with all the DLCs installed so I don't know what the game is like without the DLCs but the base game itself is massive from what I have seen. For the price and level of replayability, I would highly recommend it even at the base price but it does come on sale frequently.
