Easy contender for best rpg ever made without question. The combat feels amazing and looks beautiful. The gear progression feels well paced and offers a wonderful selection of weaponry and armor. The missions are incredibly written, causing you to be enthralled in even the most basic of errands. The enemies are fascinating, and cause me to regularly find myself reading through the beastiary just for funsies. The maps are awesome, with plenty to check out and plenty to do. And, as I am sure anybody with internet access knows by now, the game is absolutely GORGEOUS. Gwent though? Oh my god is gwent so rigged. It's like walking into a casino that doesn't even bother pretending like you could win lol. Imagine this, You spend 30 minutes going all across the map purchasing gwent cards from anyone who has some to sell. After a while you decide to use your new paper arsenal against the populace in order to take their cards too. You think about who the easiest opponent to start with would be, and eventually settle on a villager in the middle of a swamp who lives almost entirely alone. you think to yourself "what cards could this swamp man possibly have?" and prepare for an easy battle. In the first match he surprises you with a decent amount of frontline and ranged cards, but not enough to overwhelm you, and you win the round. With the first round finished, all you need to do is to place every unit card you have and overwhelm him in the the second round for the win, so you do so. in response the man places a single melee card, with a total of 6 points to offer. You may not realize in this moment, but you have already lost. Before you can think, the old man places a card that kills your highest point card. you replace it with a soldier card, its worth 1 point... Immediately after the old man drops ANOTHER death card, and kills 2 ranged cards who boosted each other up to 10 points, you lose 20... Now you have 11 points total. like a small hare struggling in the mouth of a fox as it is dragged away, you play your final unit card. like the 3 cards you still have in play, it's a ranged card. It doesn't boost anybody, or give you an extra card, just gives the 4 points, but as far as you know right now? That's enough. So you play it, and pray to whichever god you believe in. How does your god answer your prayers? The old man plays a weather card, all 4 of your ranged cards are now worth 1 point each. You have 4 points, he has 6. You have no more unit cards. He has 1 card you don't know. You think "Wait! there's no way that last card of his is a unit card, not this late in the round, it has to be a weather card or special card! this could still be a win if I use my weather card!" So you do and play your final card, now his only unit card in play is worth 1 point. "4 against 1, and there's no way you have another unit card to play, I HAVE this." you think to yourself, another false hope. The old man plays a ranged unit card, but he plays it to your side. 5 against 1 now... which would almost be a comfort, if you didn't know what comes after that is. As fast as a blink, the old man draws 2 cards from his deck... You don't manage to catch a glimpse of either one, yet you still feel the dread. With no cards to play and no other choice, you pass, and leave your fate in the old mans hands. Before you can get out a second prayer, the old man plays a siege unit card, which lays in the only part of the battlefield that remains unaffected by weather cards. It's worth 8 points. 5 against 9, it's over, it's a bust... but it isn't over, not until HE says it is. The old man plays a second siege card, it's worth 1 point, but it has a boost to other siege units. He has 12 points to your 5. You lose, and it's all your fault for your ignorance. Little did you know that this swamp man with 32 syllables in his name is actually a legend of old. He is a comic con yu-gi-oh! tournament master who retired to play gwent against the drowners in the swamps of velen. And you are just one of many victims to suffer underestimating his card fueled warpath.

博德之门 该怎么说呢，它已经不单单是一款游戏了。我初识它是在高三暑假，高考结束后的那段日子过得并不顺心，那段时间我常常会陷入迷茫，不知道活着的意义在哪，进入大学之后，日子依旧是疲惫又麻木的。一次机缘巧合，我认识了博德之门。朋友跟我说可以试一试，绝对不亏，这个游戏特别好玩。我和朋友坐在他家电脑前，第一次点开了这个后来给我带来很多盼头的游戏。 当我第一次看见塔夫的选择页面写着，这是属于你的时代，你的时代即将来临，我当时还没有意识到，这个游戏会这么尊重玩家。在玩它之前，我完全没有接触过龙与地下城、跑团这类内容，听朋友说做很多事都要过检定，还觉得有点麻烦。可真正玩进去之后，才懂其中的乐趣：你的攻击未必能命中，法术会被豁免，你甚至可以靠话术骗过别人，哪怕说辞看着很离谱。当屏幕跳出20点大成功的时候，忍不住笑出来，哈哈，大成功！这下拿我没办法啦！ 我最喜欢的是伙伴们。第一次大多是在朋友电脑上游玩，所以我自己的游玩时长算不上很多，但我真的很感谢博德之门，给了我现实里很难得到的体验。同行的伙伴会在路上拌嘴，互相评价彼此，每个人都带着独属于自己的过往。其中阿斯代伦这个角色真的塑造得太好了，谢谢创作者，打造出这样一个动人的角色。他不只是我在另一个世界里倾心的人，更像是支撑我的精神寄托。 一开始我以为他只是油嘴滑舌的贵族，看着性子跳脱，只是人设有意思。慢慢深入了解才读懂，他为什么要用花言巧语保护自己。当他被好好对待、得到尊重的时候，会愣一下，再认真地道谢；表白的时候手足无措，听到你说很在乎他，第一反应是下意识反驳。我心里一直想告诉他，你真的值得被好好爱着，不是因为容貌，也不是别的，只是希望你能做你自己，活成你想要成为的样子。 飞升的结局确实会牵连很多人，这点我清楚。但比起评判对错，我更在意他本身。他熬过了两百多年无尽的煎熬，那些痛苦我们没办法切身感受，我们没有资格替他定论，说苦难和他经历的一切可以互相抵消。我不想用世俗的道德标准捆绑他。阳光、街道、白昼本来就该属于他，是别人夺走了他享受这些的资格，这从来都不是他的错。我看完了阿斯代伦的相关外传小说，更加明白，这一切本就不是他的过错。是卡扎多尔夺走了他看见日光的权利。选择这条路线，我只是想把本该属于他的东西还给他，想让他重新沐浴在阳光下好好活着。两百多年实在太久了，陪着我们走完这一路冒险，我只希望他能遵从自己的心意做出选择，好好活下去，活得舒心。我知道另一条路线也可以慢慢寻找在日光下安稳生活的办法，但我实在不想让他继续等下去了，我想在这场冒险里，让他得到属于他的幸福。 不只是阿斯代伦，盖尔、影心、明萨拉、威尔、莱泽尔、卡拉克，全都是我在这个异世界里无比珍贵的同伴。现实里很难遇到相处起来这么舒服的人，这样的羁绊也很难拥有。这段冒险故事，好像给了我第二次人生。在这里，我可以是拯救世界的英雄，也可以是背负特殊出身、敢于挣脱命运枷锁的人；出身可以高贵，也可以平凡低微。博德之门把选择权完完整整交到玩家手上。它尊重我，也告诉我，人是拥有选择的自由的。你可以选择做善良的人，也可以选择胆小退缩，或是优先守住自己的私心，没有刻板的标尺去规定你必须怎么走。没有人规定我们一定要沿着既定的路线往前走，一定要按别人期待的轨迹生活。 因为博德之门，我慢慢去了解龙与地下城的世界观。十八岁这一年，我遇见了这个宏大、瑰丽，同时又残酷真实的世界，里面有着多样的族群、语言与神明，像一个瑰丽的梦。以前我从来没想过关于身后的事，现在我有了一个小小的心愿：如果可以，我希望之后能来到龙与地下城的世界，成为一名术士。 博德之门不只是好玩，它承载了我的另一段人生，毫无疑问，它在我心里永远是最好的游戏。 感谢拉瑞安工作室，是你们构筑出这样恢弘动人的故事，赠予我这一段别样的人生。我体会到心动的滋味，慢慢靠近在意的人，收获伙伴的祝福，和大家围坐在一起聚餐，认真和他说，我真的很在乎你，紧紧抱住他。哪怕只是隔着屏幕看见这些画面，感受却真切得仿佛亲身经历。 总而言之，博德之门3有着无可替代的同伴剧情和自由的选择分支。如果你也想要一段由自己亲手书写的旅程，不妨来试一试。 阿斯代伦，我爱你。博德之门，是我的另一个家乡

我希望第二部实现的五个突破 1. 让城市真正具备持续运行的社会生态。 帮派应当能够争夺地盘，企业行动应当产生社会后果，NPC 可以拥有可信的日常活动，玩家也应该通过行动改变自己在街区中的处境。如果你摧毁某个帮派的重要设施，该地区的势力、交易活动和安全状况应该在随后发生变化。不需要模拟每一个居民，但需要让关键行为产生持续性的世界反馈。 2. 让玩家拥有真正不同的人生。 公司特工、街头佣兵、网络黑客不应该只是技能配置不同。他们应当具备不同的信息来源、人际网络、任务解决方式和成长路径。例如同一个目标，黑客可以侵入企业网络，谈判专家能够利用利益关系，武装佣兵则选择正面突破。不过这些方案的后续代价也应有所不同。 3. 把人工智能从背景设定变成真正的系统主题。 我认为这是第二部最有机会超越第一部的方向。现实世界的生成式 AI、自动化决策、数字身份与数据所有权问题，已经让传统赛博朋克设定变得越来越接近现实。第二部完全有机会把数字人格、企业 AI、自主意识以及黑墙之外的智能实体发展成更深入的叙事主题。 4. 保留单人故事的核心价值，不要为了多人模式牺牲它。 我认为《2077》的真正竞争力是它的人物叙事，不是在线枪战。第二部可以探索可选的合作体验，但我不希望它被改造成重度在线服务型游戏，更不希望任务设计被赛季、刷取和商业化机制主导。 5. 不要盲目追求更大的地图。 如果第二部有两座城市，我希望它们在社会制度、势力关系、经济运作与角色生活方式上存在实质差异。否则，两座空洞的城市不一定胜过一座丰富的城市。我更希望 CDPR 把第二部的开发预算花在城市互动密度上，而不是继续增加无意义的地图面积。

Great game, honestly! As someone who knows the struggle of making games like this, and how hard it is to store player data and keep planets looking like planets, I think the devs did a fantastic job. I could never reach this level, even with help. The game they’ve built over 10 years is amazing. I’m a relatively new player, so I don’t know all the bits and bobs yet, but even when I’m older I bet it’ll still surprise me with new things, animals, and places. It has its glitches here and there, like the odd object floating in the air or clipping into the ground, but nothing major. Honestly, awesome game, and the devs did great to get it where it is today. The graphics are beautiful too. The colours, the skies, and the planets look stunning, and they still amaze me even though the game is 10 years old. Every time I land on a new planet I stop just to look around. There’s so much to do as well. You can explore, build bases, trade, fly around in your own ships, and play with friends in multiplayer. It even has VR support, which makes exploring feel even more real. The devs have also kept adding free updates for years, which is rare these days and shows how much they care about the game and the players. If you check my PC specs, you’ll see basic, bottom-of-the-line parts you probably wouldn’t expect. If your PC is like mine and not too great, GET THE DARN GAME! I get 60 FPS in most scenarios. If you’re worried your PC is “too bad” to run it well, don’t be. The optimization is crazy! Like I said, 60 FPS is pretty good for my PC. Seriously, get the game. It has endless fun and activities, and I’m still not bored. Trust me. Easy recommend from me! And there is so much to explore out there! But I’ll let you, whether you’re a newcomer or an old player, figure those things out for yourself. Now go and happy exploring!

# The Witcher 3 Review ## 1. Atmosphere & Level Design — 10/10 **World — 10/10:** With the remaster and what my rig can offer, I feel like I'm getting the best of everything this game has to offer visually. This remaster is exactly how I remember this game aging in my head. It is just as beautiful to play today as it was when it first came out. Every zone feels unique, and every location feels like it has a reason to exist. **Level Design — 10/10:** From swamps to cities, islands and Vikings, to France-inspired regions and wine country, every environment builds upon the world with masterful storytelling. Every area feels worth exploring and taking the time to appreciate. **Exploration — 10/10:** This game is a completionist's dream. So much to do, so much to discover, and so much to explore. ## 2. Characters & Companions — 9.33/10 **Main Character — 10/10:** Geralt is one of my favorite fictional characters. Even though we're constantly told he has no emotions, I think he displays more meaningful emotion than most characters. He's witty, sarcastic, and ultimately tries to be a force for good in a world filled with cruelty and horror. **Companions — 10/10:** There is so much lore behind every companion and character you meet. Honestly, the romance options are fantastic too. It's always difficult to choose, and that's a good problem to have. **Character Development — 8/10:** Probably the weakest point of the category. It's not necessarily that these characters evolve or develop dramatically. Many are already established, and I think there's something special about seeing them remain true to who they are. The score is an 8 because your choices can still lead to some pretty bad outcomes. That's part of what makes it an RPG. ## 3. Story — 9.67/10* **Main Story — 10/10:** I love the hunt for Ciri. Having read the books, played the other games, and watched the shows, the story feels incredibly compelling. **Writing — 10/10:** Even the DLCs are masterpieces in writing. So much of the storytelling is built around relationships, right and wrong, and the moral grounds you're willing or unwilling to stand on. **Pacing — 9/10:** The story has great pacing. As a completionist, though, F the Skellige island markers scattered across the ocean and getting stuck in the swamps. Haha. The story keeps you engaged, and there's always something to keep a completionist busy. **Ending:** The main ending is great. Hearts of Stone is amazing, and Blood and Wine is perhaps the best DLC ever made. ## 4. Combat & Gameplay — 9.75/10 **Combat — 10/10:** This is my favorite RPG combat system in any game. The modern controls and quick casting refresh were amazing. You can do so much without it feeling like a hassle, and the new finishers are fantastic. **Gameplay Loop — 10/10:** I'm a completionist. There's plenty to do. Enough said. **Progression — 9/10:** Leveling feels fair, even starting fresh on Death March. My only complaint is that I found it nearly impossible to acquire all the ability points needed for the additional mutagens and slots, even after completing the main game and both DLCs. I also wasn't able to craft every Grandmaster gear set, only the two I was testing builds with. **Variety — 10/10:** I never really felt bored playing this game, with the exception of those Skellige question marks out in the ocean. # Final Score Atmosphere & Level Design: 10/10 Characters & Companions: 9.33/10 Story: 9.67/10* Combat & Gameplay: 9.75/10 **Overall: 9.69/10** **Final Thoughts:** This is probably not even a top five game for me, but it's definitely top three. Even then, it might actually take the top spot as my favorite video game of all time. Hundreds of hours across PS4, Xbox, and now Steam. I've finally gotten around to reviewing it.

Thank you for giving a disgruntled Pokémon fan what Nintendo never could This game blends creature collection, survival mechanics and exploration wonderfully, and the progression feels pretty good outside of the late game technology point grind. All of the systems, though some can certainly be a pain at first (climate, food decay, weapon repairs), can all be managed reasonably or mitigated somewhat through abilities and items. The base creation, while seemingly limited at first due to the small size of the given building space, takes off once you realize the vertical potential. However, some of the bigger pals clip through tight rooms and areas, which can be a little off-putting at best, and downright criminal at worst. (the pals can get very large) Overall, while I am not completely finished with the game, I've enjoyed it significantly more than I thought I would, and I absolutely recommend it to anyone who enjoyed Pokémon in the past, as well as anyone else interested.

So, Halo. The legendary series known far and wide that singlehandedly sold millions of Xboxes. In spite of the series eventually being handed off to 343 and put through the world's slowest suicide, the first 4 games are still universally beloved to this day. Unfortunately though, as someone who never grew up with them with no hype to cloud my vision, the series is just good and not great. You can respect something for its innovations and what it did to the industry, but the games themselves are extremely basic, poorly balanced shooters that were just vehicles to sell the multiplayer. They're not bad by any stretch, but compared to many many other shooters that came later, time has not been kind to them. These games also lose points in my eyes for prototyping things like sitting in cover doing nothing to recharge your shields in the gameplay, and snarky, arrogant and insufferable girlbosses (at least 1 per game) in the story. (But mercifully half of the latter do get killed off. ) Halo: CE: The game that started it all. Clunky voice acting, an extremely basic story that completely shifts gears halfway through and a sombre ending that gets retconned immediately, mixed with a combat system with nothing really to offer veterans of the genre. All of the enemies are ridiculous damage sponges, to the point where it feels like every gun but the sniper, shotgun and rocket launcher shoot feathers. The level design is horrible, with hour long levels where you walk through the same 3 rooms and hallways over and over and over again followed by massive open areas with no cover, with enemy placements that feel like the devs just tossed 10 enemies into an enclosed space and called it a day. The checkpoints are extremely far apart, with a single random grenade falling off a grunt one-shotting you and costing you minutes of progress for no reason. You have a flimsy health bar that doesn't recharge like the rest of the series, and health packs are unbelievably sparce. I normally play shooters on hard mode, but I had to switch to normal to have any enjoyment whatsoever without my badass armored super-soldier dying from a stiff breeze. Halo 2: marked improvements to the gameplay (like dual-wielding) and story, but still nothing groundbreaking. You actually find out who and what the covenant are in-game without being forced to read a book, and it's actually compelling. Playing as Arbiter for half the game is novel, but him and chief are nearly identical in every way apart from flashlight/cloak, so they feel more similar than they should. Guns still shoot feathers and the enemies are still stupidly tanky, and in the latter half of the game, nearly all of the enemies are brutes, which makes the tankiness even worse. The game also had an extremely troubled production back in the day, and as such, the game just ends on a massive cliffhanger basically out of nowhere. Halo 3: The best game in terms of gameplay and story. Guns actually feel marginally powerful, and combat gadgets allow you to get more creative with your gameplay and positioning. The levels are well designed, combat feels good, the locales are varied, and the story comes to a pretty satisfying conclusion assuming you deem everything afterward non-canon like most fans do. ODST: a brief spinoff that takes place between 2 and 3 starring a crack team of boring jabronies. Half the game is spent wandering through the same 3 dark, empty streets as a silent protag, maybe shooting 2 or 3 enemies before going into a flashback that plays out like a proper mission. (A very short mission, and then it's back to wandering in the dark again for the same amount of time.) It is PAINFULLY boring, and it's a story that didn't need to be told as the only thing you learn is that the snail-iens that you've been shooting all game are actually snail-frens. That's it. Master Chief is not even mentioned once, and you only briefly hear from one of the jabroni squad again in Reach. Completely pointless. Halo: Reach: A prequel to CE. The gameplay is "modernized" for lack of a better term, with the gimmick being armor abilities like sprinting, cloak and invincibility instead of them being powerups. The gameplay is about tied with 3 in terms of quality, and all of the characters don't get nearly enough dialogue or screentime for me to care about any of them. The game is mostly famous for its ending and how it immediately leads into the first game, but apart from that it's a pretty unncessessary prequel that still doesn't even explain why the covenent are at war with humanity in the first place. Best get reading, idiot. Halo 4: I didn't play it. I've heard that everything after 3 sucks and the story careens off a cliff, so I'm not wasting my time. There are far worse shooters out there, and if you want to see how the genre were revolutionized back in the day, they are still enjoyable. They are still good games that paved the way for what came after, but without growing up with them, they don't even come close to my favorites of the genre.

This is the greatest game ever made. Insane levels of depth and is really rewarding for hardcode players. There is incredible diversity in how people approach builds. poe.ninja's ladder indexes thousands of people. Every league you can find someone high up on the ladder who is using a trash skill and finding the 3 or 4 mechanics they can combine to make it worthwhile. One thing I saw this league was lightning warp + max duration in order to run heist efficiently. Very pro-player developers. Leagues are every 3 months and provide tons of new content, balance updates, and a fresh economy. After those 3 months, your characters and items are sent to "standard league" which is the permanent league where tons of legacy versions of items are floating around. It's an amazing way to keep things fresh and I've never quite seen a game that operates around a set schedule like this. Every new league launch PoE hits top player numbers on Steam and gets a wave of hype. The only thing that's not great about PoE is the new player experience. As a new player you are going to have absolutely no idea what you are doing, and your build is going to suck. You'll probably have to restart in order to get a build that can finish the campaign. And most experienced PoE players consider the campaign to be like "the tutorial". Mapping is where the real game starts and opens up all of the endgame strategies and content.

elden ring was a game that took me an embarrassingly long time to get into, thanks to its overwhelmingly large world, the absurd difficulty of the bosses and enemies, and a complete lack of any exposition whatsoever. I had no motivation to push further into the game, to give it the time necessary to understand what made it special, and i regret not getting into it sooner. elden ring is one of the best games I've ever played, it uses a colossal open world and a completely hands-off approach to the player's exploration and development of strategies/builds to let you grow and take on its daunting obstacles and challenges by any means necessary. i had assumed for the longest time that fromsoft games were just harsh challenges that asked the player to meet an uncompromising obstacle and tackle it exactly as it is, and to some extent thats true. bosses in elden ring have a fixed difficulty in the way that their health, attack patterns, and damage dealt cannot be changed, they exist as they are, and you have to find a way to defeat them. the change in difficulty instead comes from the player and your own progression, with complete freedom in what level you tackle the boss at, and what kind of items, spells, or spirit ashes you'll use for the fight you can almost always find a strategy to counter any boss, and a way to take an impossible fight and make it something manageable. i barely struggled any more than i needed to, and always found myself taking on bosses that i would be evenly matched with and able to reasonably beat (most bosses took maybe an hour tops, with the toughest taking multiple sessions but rarely more than maybe 4-5 hours total (except for the valiant gargoyles)). due to a lack of a strict narrative or proper exposition, the game allows the exploration to become the main point of the game, with whatever knowledge you gain as you wander forming your primary understanding of the world, letting the experience vary drastically from person to person. vague spoilers for the endings: it's only fitting that the choices you make and the endings of the game end up being heavily symbolic and vague, you wander a ruined and decaying world, so of course when it hits a breaking point, you get to decide what direction it goes into, whether to maintain the status quo with you on top, to simply burn it all down, or the most popular choice: to bring about a change so radical that the world will be unrecognizable from what it was before . that exploration and deeply personal narrative and decision making allows for a level of investment and attachment that really make the game unforgettable. my first playthrough took a solid 160 hours and for the entire duration i was excited to keep pushing forward, the world stayed mysterious and dangerous and interesting, there is honestly nothing like it. i think its worth checking out. to say the least.

I bought this game when it originally came out and was so thoroughly disappointed that it was the last preorder I ever made. Now, I wait days after reviews drop to ensure I never run into that issue again. Everything people were saying about the game back then was completely true. It felt incomplete, grindy as all hell, and you ran out of things to do as soon as you reached the final story mission. What’s funny is that most of those criticisms are still somewhat true: the game can still feel grindy, the campaign still feels a little incomplete, and the gameplay loop can feel kinda rote by your 40th hour. What hooks me now, though, is the massive amount of content added through updates and expansions, along with all the custom sliders. You can tune it into a hardcore space sim or turn down the difficulty and resource management to play it as a cozy, low-punishment game. At the end of the day, I keep coming back for the procedural generation of planets and activities, as well as some of the most beautiful visual sights you can see every time you boot it up. My opinion of Sean Murray has come full circle—I hate him now for a completely different reason: he won't let me give him more money after a decade of free updates!

Ready or Not offers a different kind of experience compared to most shooters, and I really enjoy the tactical approach it takes. It's overall a reasonably good game with most of its systems being well-fleshed out. However, the balancing needs some work, and the enemy AI needs to have their crack taken away. It's been almost 3 years now, people have been constantly telling VOID that the AI are skynet terminators, and they have stubbornly refused to acknowledge this and fix them. So I'll stubbornly refuse to give this otherwise good game a positive review, because it is ruined by atrocious AI, which become way worse on Hard difficulty and require bug abuse or incredible luck to finish missions. Other problems include the SWAT AI being complete nincompoops by comparison, excessive suppression effects on the player yet enemies suffer no such thing as suppression, ridiculous and unrealistic weapon sway while moving, no rubber bullets for the dozens of guns we have, some traps being virtually invisible and impossible to manually disarm (either due to being hard to see or because some particular doors don't swing out far enough), bomb vest suspects can still get animation locked (stun one by any means, then start disarming the bomb before they recover), and there really isn't a good reason why we should have to take terrorists alive; and any armed suspect in general conscious; for the best score. Many of the missions also don't have great variety and some missions are more linear than they really need to be, especially Relapse. If you're going to make it so that players have to restart a mission over and over again to clear it, why not at least allow for more variety and routes? Finally, the DLC are overpriced and the base game doesn't really have enough content to justify buying at full price. No, the taser does not need to be nerfed again. It was fine after the first time, stop nerfing it.

⭐ Not Recommended – One of the Most Overrated Games I've Ever Played I genuinely refuse to believe people enjoy playing this game. At this point, I'm convinced the 10/10 reviews are part of some elaborate social experiment. Let's start with the horse. Apparently, riding a horse requires a fucking PhD. Why does something as simple as travelling from A to B feel like I'm trying to land a Boeing 747? The horse has the intelligence of a potato and controls like it's actively working against me. The controls are an absolute fucking joke. There are approximately 7,000 different keybinds, none of which seem to have been designed by someone who has actually used a keyboard before. Every five seconds I'm having to Google what button does what because apparently remembering 400 different inputs is now a core gameplay mechanic. And the tutorial? What tutorial? Apparently Rockstar expects you to absorb the entire control scheme through psychic communication. Controller aiming is somehow even worse. Trying to shoot something feels like attempting brain surgery while wearing boxing gloves. I want to aim at an enemy, not negotiate a peace treaty with the right analogue stick. And the graphics? Don't get me wrong, they're decent, but holy shit, you'd think this game was rendering the actual universe with the amount of resources it consumes. My PC is working overtime to deliver an experience that looks nowhere near worth the performance hit. I keep hearing about this incredible masterpiece, but so far I've experienced: A horse with the handling characteristics of a shopping trolley. Controls designed by someone who clearly hates human hands. Aiming that makes me question whether my controller is broken. An unnecessary amount of keybinds. Performance demands that would make NASA reconsider its budget. Apparently, the story is amazing. Fantastic. Unfortunately, I have to PLAY the game to experience it, and playing it feels like an unpaid administrative job. I don't care how beautiful the sunsets are or how realistic the horse's testicles supposedly are. If I need a fucking instruction manual to get on a horse and shoot someone, something has gone horribly wrong. Red Dead Redemption 2: 10/10 cinematic experience, 2/10 actual gameplay experience. I wanted to play a cowboy game, not become a full-time horse technician with a minor in keyboard memorisation. I genuinely don't understand the hype.

More than just a Ghost Hunting Game. With over 1,000 hours on Xbox and another 400+ hours here on PC, I think it's safe to say Phasmo has become much more than a game to me. I never imagined how much of an impact this game would have on my life back when i first started playing. What started as a game where I would run into the house to swear at the ghosts, then get scared and immediately run back outside... turned into making countless friendships and opportunities I don't think I would've experienced otherwise. There's so many incredible people I've met through Phasmo, some of who we played together nearly every night for months. So many funny moments and memories I'll carry with me for a long time. But one of the biggest things Phasmo has done for me is help shape my streaming journey. This game played a huge role in getting me into content creation, building a community, and eventually achieving something I once thought was out of reach- becoming a Twitch Partner. It also opened the door to discovering other horror games as well, meeting other creators, which has led me to to becoming content creator and partner for other games. No game is perfect of course. There will always be things that can be improved, but when I look at the big picture, it's hard not to appreciate everything this game has done for me. To the developers at Kinetic Games- thank you for everything!

Never thought I'd really enjoy a roguelike as much as I dig Darkest Dungeon at this point. The story is simple and blunt, your goal given right on without too much context about everything. And given the focus of the game is the gameplay and about dungeon exploring, this is perfectly fine. The graphics and music has a dark atmosphere in general, enhancing the setting and giving it the right vibes for the gloomy and dark situations you're getting thrown in. The art style has its nice and recognizable way to make the trips into the dungeons and explore those a good experience overall. Given the genre, it's a repetitive cycle of you preparing your characters for the next exploration trip, expand your options in town to make them stronger, make services cheaper, and giving you better odds at not running into misery. Many classes to pick and build your teams around, themed teams for specific dungeon types making things a bit easier within those. Given the amount of skills every class has, you can go with different approaches and builds for them, not being a one-way ticket to only get used as a tank but a tank also able to go into an offensive build if you like this approach more. Dungeon exploration is a matter how many items you took with you and into what obstacles you'll run eventually. Dungeon designs randomized, some dungeons ending up with a more tedious room layout, some on the straight and simple progression. Resource management will decide how decent or not a trip will be, gathering items to sell or collect for town upgrades, making decisions what to keep and what to drop as the inventory isn't the biggest. Quest tasks vary from exploring the whole dungeon to find specific objects to interact or to collect, different sizes and difficulties for the dungeons existing. Battles are in general RPG style, choosing the skills you want to use, having specific ranges or positions you have to be in to use those. Hit and dodge chances giving everything an RNG touch while turn order also not solely relying on one stat but also has some RNG to it included. Enemy variation is big enough to not feel like you run into the same enemies over and over while different areas have a focus on specific enemy types. Your characters will get stressed and once too stressed, things could go 180 and make a run more complicated. With how much RNG is included within passives, status effects, and many more, the runs you expect to be easy may still turn something into results not expected, making it fun despite you doing these runs constantly. Difficulty for the game is to me in the mid-levels, some enemies being on the comfier side to deal with while some will give you some headaches. Bosses do something annoying and even nasty, learning about those things when encountering those. And given a character's death is permanent, you have to make the right decisions whether to continue or be safe and bail out of a dungeon before worse happens. The game plays a lot of mind games with you and your decisions, but I didn't feel anything was overly difficult to even unfair. You can adapt to situations and areas with the right setups so things will get easier if you know what you do. What increased my experience by a lot is how much the modding scene has to offer for the game. I only knew a few skins for classes to exist which were the reason why I got mildly interested in DD in the beginning, but once I saw what options I have and what modders created over the last decade, I've found a lot of visual changes which made the game a feast for my eyes. New classes, skins for those, many ways to tweak your game and experience it with a new touch. Not to mention that you can tweak a few things by yourself rather easy once figuring out which files are for what. I've made a few changes to my NPCs myself, and will surely do more of that in the future. Negatives about the game? The usual easy to learn, and hard to master mentality comes into play for sure. It took some hours to get a gist of how to operate my runs, what options I have to make them a bit comfier, and what can wreck you and what to look out for. I personally felt that the passives you may get after a successful run more often than not went into the negatives, receiving more bad passives over good ones, but there's eventually a mod to balance that out a bit more. Not sure if it's intended like that but felt a bit more geared towards receiving some bad passives, but could just be me not having the best luck with those. Expect to curse a lot when your 90%+ hit chances end up in missing enemies, or you getting smacked into dangerous levels out of nowhere which can be funny in a grim way~ I'm usually not much into roguelikes, but the combination of how I can tweak the game to my liking plus the bit I've seen and knew about the game got me into giving it a try. Which resulted in my little issue to pick from a very few roguelikes to play whenever time and mood allows it to now being settled into these dungeons. To me, there's no real finish to the game, a lot of things you can do and also add with the help of mods to have a reason to come back whenever you desire. And when on sale, it's just a few bucks which is a lot you get out for such little investment. I like my games with clear goals and beating them, but this game is now fully accepted by me to come back to and enjoy the game.

I love this game. Been playing this game for more than 4,500 hours (PvE, solo). This review is aimed at the changes in the Enhanced version, not the game in general. TL;DR: Superficially nice, but it offers nothing the legacy version doesn't have. (UI Slider?!? devs, hello?) I stayed with the legacy version for a long time because I hesitated to set up my modlist every time they release a new engine update. Now I decided to make the switch a few days ago, but I am not excited about the Enhanced version at all. The new graphics look really nice, but that's it. The shadows and lighting create an uncomfortable environment that is almost painful to play in for longer than a few minutes. It looks nice in the trailers, but actual gameplay is more than uncomfortable. Worst of all is the UI. Everything in the HUD is way too small, except the Journey steps, which obscure half of the screen. On the other hand, everything in the Inventory and Knowledge tabs is HUGE. The icons are way too big, making the whole interface feel almost claustrophobic. It feels like a lazy mobile or console layout forced onto Pc players. WHY is there no UI size slider? I'll never understand how in the world game developers can basically create a new version of a game but completely ignore such a crucial element like the UI. Even worse, they didn't include any UI scaling whatsoever, leaving PC players completely stranded. EDIT: I almost forgot. Why does the camera zoom in and out like crazy when i have target lock activated? What in the world is this supposed to archieve? The only thing it causes is motion sickness. (Keep it as it was before. IT WAS FINE!!) I have no idea what's going on with the devs of this game, but these things are the OPPOSITE of improvements. THIS is why i do not recommend the game.

What I love most about Civ VI is the amount of control and meaningful decisions it gives me. I enjoy expanding aggressively in the early game, securing territory, building defensible borders and preparing for potential wars. Then comes my favorite part: developing those settlements into powerful, specialized cities while carefully balancing food, production, gold, science and culture. Managing builders, assigning citizens to specific tiles, planning districts and optimizing individual cities might seem like unnecessary micromanagement to some, but to me, that's the heart of Civilization. Every little decision contributes to something bigger. You're not just watching an empire grow; you're building it yourself. The real enjoyment comes from developing an empire and competing with other civilizations throughout history. Civ VI wasn't perfect at launch. I initially found its art style a little goofy, and I believe some of the content introduced through expansions should have been part of the base game. I'm not a fan of games relying on paid DLC to feel complete. However, Rise and Fall and Gathering Storm helped turn an already enjoyable game into something truly exceptional. Playing Civilization VII has actually made me appreciate Civ VI even more. While VII introduces some interesting ideas, I feel that too many meaningful decisions have been simplified, automated or removed entirely. Losing builders, manual tile management and much of the freedom I had when developing my empire has reminded me why I enjoyed the previous games so much. I don't need a Civilization game to be more complicated just for the sake of complexity. I want the freedom to make meaningful decisions and experience the consequences of those decisions throughout thousands of years of history. That's what Civilization VI does so well!! It's not about winning as quickly as possible. It's about taking a single settler, founding a civilization, shaping its history and eventually looking across the map at an empire that exists because of the choices you made. Civilization VI isn't perfect, but it's a fantastic strategy game, and one I can happily spend another thousand hours playing.

First thing to be said is that this game works really bad on modern RTX cards since the first thing you notice is that skybox and light is flickering. The FPS is kinda low and doesn't change with different presets. So you need to install mods to make it work properly! From cold Chicago we go to sunny San Francisco. The game changes its tone and it seems both in story and gameplay. The story now feels less serious and depressing which is not bad but also more global. Now we follow not only revenge but we change society. In the first game you was following Aiden's storyline but here I can highlight DedSec as a main character. Marcus in just a part of something bigger while he is still controlled by player. There are several characters that Marcus works and each of them has their own style and attributes that are memorable. The game itself is a satire on modern society with AI and Big Brother that is watching your every step which is aged well and actual in 2026. Gameplaywise this game has better hacking and world interaction than the previous one. Now we can use RC and Drone to solve different riddles and neutralise enemies. Now you can make different gangs fight each other or even call cops on someone you don't like just by getting skill in a skilltree. In this game you have different approach to your enemies: you can hack them through cameras, use drone or RC, just shoot or use environment to neutralise them. Also interactions with the world are cool and npcs react on your actions. One of my favourite things are hacking riddles - there are plenty of them during the story and on the map and many of them make you think. To be honest shooting is not the strongest part of the game. You don't have slow motion like in the first game and you don't really feel the impact of the guns. Visuals are incredible sometimes the game looks very realistic and thats the 2016 game!!! Online here is more alive that in the first game and much funnier too! I really love this game and if you liked the first one you should try the second part!

I will mainly be talking about the single-player, so up to this day the GTA I liked the least among Vice City, IV and San Andreas I am not taking into account the 2D era. To begin, the story is heavily inspired by heist movies like Heat. You take control of three criminals who have to carry out a marathon of robberies against a backdrop of conflicts and unspoken tensions. The gameplay in the chase sequences is completely scripted. The story is simple and not memorable; the writing is decent, but we're still looking for iconic characters with cheeky lines. I wonder where Rockstar Games' humor has gone. The characters are all bland and lack personality; it's more hipster writing than what we're used to seeing. The fact that you can play as three characters simultaneously is something I didn't like because it breaks a certain dynamic, and the characters are less developed. I'm not interested in playing as Franklin, who isn't developed at all. I was really disappointed by the lack of missions in his neighborhood and with his gang. He has an immeasurable lack of charisma. He's practically erased from the story. If I'd had the choice to kill him at the end, I would have chosen him without a doubt. Trevor, on the other hand, is a good character that I wish I hadn't played as, but rather visited for missions. I compare him to Phil Cassidy, a bit of a crazy guy. Trevor was added during development, according to Dan Houser, there was no intention of controlling him. That shows how underdeveloped the story is. The real and best-developed character is Michael (inspired by Tony Soprano's life), the most interesting because he has a connection to the ghetto through Franklin and to the desert/country through Trevor. It's Michael who connects people; he's the most charismatic character and the one who truly carries GTA V, in addition to having impeccable voice acting. A GTA without DLC, with far less missions (79 missions) than San Andreas (101 missions) and GTA IV + DLCs (136 missions), a little over 10 more missions than Vice City (67 missions), a game from 2002. Isn't there a slight problem considering we play as three characters? The late 2010s, with Rockstar Games and Take-Two influencing the video game world, marked the beginning of an era where studios focused on online play, where fewer and fewer people played single-player games. As a result, we ended up with games where single-player was neglected in favor of online mode, as perfectly exemplified by GTA V. In the 2000s, multiplayer appeared in the menu after the single-player campaign; today, games shove online mode right in your face. Studios that have become focused solely on online play, a lack of single-player DLC, microtransactions, endless updates, and an over-exploitation of online mode given the profit it generates. Red Dead Redemption 2 is the exception, but keep in mind that it's the only Rockstar game developed for 4th-generation consoles. The online mode was cool in the early years because it focused on creating lasting memories. You can't take that away from them. But the writing is gone, the online experience has become terrible, and the people in charge of the script are a disgrace. It's worth noting that they censored original content from the solo; if you want to see the list, it's amusing. They believe they have the right to change the game because it is offensive. The fact that GTA is the most played and best-selling game of all time attracts people who don't intend to play a game, but to control it. So I'm asking for all the grafitti to be removed from the game because I feel bad against. Seriously, no jokes, this is getting ridiculous. It's the same reason I'm not playing the remastered versions of the 3D trilogy. Rockstar Games has lost many people since its creation who were part of its DNA. I'm thinking of Dan Houser, Leslie Benzies, Jamie King, Terry Donovan, Lazlow Jones, Michael Unsworth, Rupert Humphries, David Jones, Obbe Vermeij ...

It's also quite impressive how the developers keep pumping out quality content and new mechanics every season, giving players new things to interact with without making older content obsolete. The devs are also pretty smart when it comes to planning their expansions so they don't overlap with PoE 2. This way, you'll have a steady supply of PoE crack all year round. My main issue is having to replay the whole damn campaign for what feels like the 50th time. But I also understand why they do it: it forces you to become more familiar with your build, experiment with different setups, and maybe even come up with something innovative. I highly recommend this game, especially if you already have experience with this genre of games

**Rust: The Only Game Where Trust Issues Are a Survival Skill. 😂🔥** Rust isn't just a game. It's an emotional roller coaster disguised as a survival simulator. You start with a rock, a torch, and big dreams. A few hours later, you've built a fortress, collected enough loot to feel like a king, and convinced yourself you're finally safe. Then some naked guy with a spear reminds you that nothing in Rust belongs to you. You're just borrowing it until someone raids you. 😂 The PvP is intense, the base building is addictive, and the adrenaline rush when you're carrying a full inventory of loot back to your base is unmatched. Every encounter is a gamble. Every alliance is questionable. And every friendly voice outside your door is probably plotting something. I've played plenty of games, but Rust hits differently. It's brutal, unpredictable, hilarious, frustrating, and somehow keeps you coming back for more. **10/10 — Would lose everything, question humanity, and rebuild again.** Trust nobody. Protect your loot. And remember... offline doesn't mean safe. ☠️🔥

Sure buddy. Secondly, that got me thinking about the content they give to us. Look, we have an objectively unpolished game with a lot of bugs, unstable performance and literally an incomplete city, there are still many unfinished areas. However, they gradually grow on you, and the game starts to feel more beginner-friendly, with each branch of progression,Units,buildingsmechanics being relatively easier to identify and navigate. There are also more varied interactions and unique mechanics for each civilization, which was one of my biggest complaints about Civ 5. On top of that, you have more unique actions available for different units and buildings or Civ, which helps break up the tedious cycle of "press next turn until you can actually do something." What I appreciate the most, though, are the quotes that accompany technology unlocks. They feel much more noticeable and memorable than they did in Civ 5. But the music felt a bit on the weaker side maybe i was not paying attention to it as much. The game rules and modifiers are also a welcome addition, as they introduce some much-needed chaos and variety. The most annoying mechanic I've encountered so far is the World Council, which becomes available quite early but has barely any noticeable impact until around the midgame and the global warming mechanic with the floods but the natural disasters and zombies are quite funny. The map generation also feels somewhat lacking but as usual, mods can fix most of these complaints, and some of them introduce much-desired QoL improvements. I hope the developers take note and implement some of these features in their future games. It seems to be a recurring pattern where they overlook certain UI elements or fail to provide enough context on how particular mechanics are can to work.

From a rocky start to a top-tier action RPG: Amazing redemption, but still room for polish. Cyberpunk 2077 hardly needs an introduction: it’s an immersive first-person action-RPG set in the visually stunning, cutthroat metropolis of Night City. You play as V, a mercenary navigating a high-stakes story alongside Johnny Silverhand, building your character through cyberware, stealth, hacking, and intense gunplay. A Remarkable Comeback CD Projekt RED deserves huge credit for how far this game has come. Thanks to major updates —most notably Patch 2.0—alongside the wave of hype from the Edgerunners anime, the game was truly given a second life. Today, it stands as a fantastic title that fully proves its worth. Why It's Great Today: Playstyle Variety: There are so many distinct ways to play. Whether you prefer pure netrunning, stealth, melee combat, or heavy firearms, the build progression feels deep and rewarding. Night City remains one of the most impressively detailed and atmospheric open worlds in gaming history. What Keeps It From Absolute Perfection: Even though the game is in a great place, for a flagship AAA title, there are still minor physics details, vehicle interactions, and small technical quirks that could use one final polish update. Fleshing out these subtle environmental and mechanical details would truly elevate the overall immersion to the highest level. Cyberpunk 2077 is a reborn masterpiece that is well worth your time and money. While we know major content additions have wrapped up, here's hoping CD Projekt RED might still drop a future update focused on these small micro-fixes to leave the game in absolute peak condition. Highly recommended!

9/10: Awesome game!! I honestly can't believe I haven't left a review for this game yet. My one issue with Terraria is it can be rather grindy at times, especially if you want a specific item or weapon and sometimes the bosses can feel a little unfair when playing by yourself. Other than that, there is a reason it's been around for over 15 years and remains peak. The Villager Npc's feel a lot more than just shopkeepers having histories, lore, and even relationships with the other villagers. (which I love despite making it sometimes hard to plan houses for them all). This is definitely a game to play WITH friends, but can be just as fun with yourself. The vast amount of bosses, and weapons you can use to disperse them are definitely a huge plus, allowing for creative and often absurd solutions that fit for your playing style. I won't deny that you likely do need a wiki for progression or crafting while planning as while as cool as this game is, I won't deny that it isn't the most beginner friendly. (Personally I like that though). I feel it has a lot to offer, whether its building beautiful castles and creations, or battling against cosmic entities, or a fishing sim, there is something for everyone!

One of the best roguelikes and one of the only ones I've been properly able to get into. The gameplay is simple, but hard to master. It has lot of variety with lots of different bosses and routes that you do with all the different characters who all feel unique. Progression stills exists hundreds of hours into gameplay as you steadily build up unlocks which keep things fresh and entertaining even after getting every ending. The difficulty remains constant throughout the game with careful gameplay being rewarded with more chances to get powerful items and clever item choices being rewarded with easier gameplay. The sound design and music are also good which makes the whole experience even better. Everything works together really well; the only problems I have are that some items don't really synergise with others as well as they should and it can be really hard to see the shadows for enemies that drop from the sky. These can both be fixed with mods though. The game also has a story which isn't anything revolutionary, but still pretty good. The story is primarily illustrated through the theming of the different items and some short cutscenes. It's what gives the game it's unique identity and contributes towards it's deserved status as one of the classics of the genre or perhaps even the medium as a whole.

Cyberpunk 2077 hadir dengan premis naratif yang kuat dan eksekusi dunia yang solid, meskipun sempat melalui rilis awal yang penuh kacau. Daya tarik utama game ini sekarang terletak pada bagaimana CD Projekt Red konsisten merawat dan memperbaiki gamenya secara transparan. Mereka tidak membiarkan komunitasnya mati begitu saja setelah sempat hancur lebur (POIN TERBAIK UNTUK CDPR), melainkan membuktikan komitmen lewat perbaikan total hingga versi terbarunya berdiri sebagai sebuah masterpiece. Contoh paling nyatanya bisa dilihat dari stabilitas teknis di PC yang baik, berkurangnya bug gajelas, serta rombakan besar pada sistem combat, perks, dan Relic skills baru yang bikin kustomisasi build karakter makin seru. Dari segi progres dan cerita, game ini menawarkan struktur naratif yang berkesan mendalam, terbukti dari total waktu main saya yang menyentuh angka 31 jam untuk menamatkan main story, DLC Phantom Liberty, dan sekitar 50% side quest (banyak banget side questnya). Perjalanan V dari awal menapaki kerasnya Night City hingga terseret konspirasi biochip Relic diracik dengan pacing emosional yang pas. Dinamika hubungan antara V dan Johnny Silverhand membuat alur utamanya hidup dan tidak terasa hampa. Terlebih lagi, pengalaman bermain game ini terasa semakin emosional dan perfectly nice setelah menonton serial anime Cyberpunk: Edgerunners setiap sudut jalanan Night City, mulai dari distrik Megabuilding hingga bar Afterlife, terasa punya nyawa dan sejarah kelamnya sendiri. (Ada soundtrack anime yang masuk sebagai lagu, well played) Namun, puncak emosi dan nilai plus terbesar bagi saya pribadi terletak pada DLC Phantom Liberty dan dinamika karakternya, terutama Songbird/Song Seon-mi. Sejak awal, meskipun saya merasa ada gelagat yang janggal dan mencurigakan dari gerak-geriknya, kedekatan emosional membuat saya memilih untuk tetap bersama songbird. Saya mengabaikan segalapilihan berkhianat pada songbird di situasi apapun. Pilihan saya itu tetap setia di sampingnya sampai titik darah penghabisan, ngelewatin ketegangan dikejar agen NUSA, hingga benar-benar mengantarkannya terbang ke bulan. Momen perpisahan itu terasa sangat tulus, pilu, dan membekas sebagai salah satu cerita terbaik yang pernah saya mainkan. ( ini terlalu subjektif karena saya emang cinta mati sama karakter Songbird pada saat pertama kali bertemu, Asian Supremacy) Melihat kualitas fondasi dunianya yang imersif ditambah dukungan jangka panjang yang solid dari sang developer, game ini jelas sangat layak dicoba. Perlu diingat, game ini menawarkan pengalaman emosional yang luar biasa bagi pemain yang fokus ke cerita. Kalau ada diskon wajib di beli bersama DLC Phantom Liberty-nya. Good Job CDPR! I've been playing Counter-Strike for many years, and CS:GO will always be my favorite game of all time. Across multiple Steam accounts, I've probably accumulated around 8,000 hours or more in CS:GO and another 2,000 hours in CS2. Since CS2 has replaced CS:GO, it's naturally become one of my most-played and favorite games. That being said, I'm disappointed to say that I still think CS:GO felt much better overall. There's just something missing from CS2. In my opinion, the subtick system is a failure and often feels worse than what we had before. I also believe removing the in-game community server browser was a terrible decision. That's not to say CS2 doesn't have its redeeming qualities, because it certainly does. I love the new smoke mechanics, and I appreciate how much more consistent grenade jump throws are without the need for binds, especially for newer players. The menus look much better and are easier to navigate, the game obviously looks and sounds better, and there are plenty of new settings that are much easier to access without having to use the console. I don't think people should stop downloading or giving CS2 a chance. You can be sure I'll always keep coming back to it. Every time I launch the game and play a few matches, I have a great time. However, I can't help but feel that the game that replaced CS:GO, my favorite game of all time, should play and feel a little better than it currently does. That's why I'm leaving a negative review. Not because I want to turn people away from the game, but because I genuinely believe the developers can do better, and they've shown in the past that they're capable of it.

I started this game thinking, "Hmm... I don't think I'm good enough for a Souls game." Until one day, I said, NAY! I MUST! And thus, Elden Ring became not only my first FromSoftware game, but also my first ever Souls game. Initially, I spent an embarrassingly long time trying to decide which starting class to pick. Then a friend suggested, "Let's go Wretch." And I thought, screw it. Let's go. What followed was a rather interesting adventure of finding anything that moved, hitting it with a club, almost killing it, only for it to turn around and say, "Surprise MF!" Cue the words YOU DIED appearing on my screen so many times that they might as well have been permanently engraved into my soul. But then, somewhere around level 20, I finally managed to kill that golden fella on the horse. And something clicked. That one victory kickstarted what would become one of, if not THE best gaming experiences I've ever had. The feeling of finding a boss, getting absolutely demolished, coming back for revenge, getting demolished AGAIN, and repeating that cycle until you finally land the killing blow... Aaaaaah. Nothing beats it. The adrenaline rush, the satisfaction, the sheer disbelief when a boss that has been bullying you for the past two hours finally falls. I came into this game wondering if I was good enough. I left knowing that I was stubborn enough. And honestly? I'd happily die another thousand times just to experience that first victory all over again.

Rating: 9/10 Elden Ring is an extraordinary gaming experience, and one that's difficult to put into words. Its world-building and level design are nothing short of outstanding. The map is massive and constantly subverts your expectations. Just when you think you've reached the end, it keeps expanding with new regions and massive underground areas. Every location feels distinct, and the art direction is phenomenal. The graphics are solid, too. I played this completely blind, exploring and clearing almost every corner of the map over 180 hours, and I was constantly mesmerized by just how beautiful the environments looked. It doesn't rely on heavily cinematic set pieces to impress you; the sheer scale and design of the world do that on their own. It's undoubtedly a game that will go down in gaming history. The difficulty might seem intimidating at first, but the open-world design gives you plenty of freedom to tackle its challenges your own way. Whether it's experimenting with different weapons, trying out magic, or making use of Ashes of War, there's no shortage of ways to approach combat. Personally, I stuck to a single weapon and a shield, focusing on mastering the core melee combat with strength build. The bosses are mostly fantastic, with Malenia being an absolute standout. However, I do have one major complaint: the delayed attacks. Some bosses hold their swings for an absurdly long time, seemingly just to catch you mid-dodge. It feels more like an artificial way of increasing difficulty than a genuinely challenging attack pattern. Normal enemies also get a bit repetitive, but it never really bothered me. Story-wise, it follows the classic FromSoftware formula. You're not spoon-fed the plot, but if you pay attention to the world, its characters, and the environmental clues, it's fairly easy to piece things together. The questlines are fun to figure out, although the clues about where to go next can sometimes be frustratingly vague. The deep lore is brought to life through excellent voice acting and an amazing soundtrack that perfectly complements the scale of the world. As for the ending, I understand and appreciate FromSoftware's minimalist approach to storytelling, so I wouldn't call it a major disappointment, but it did leave me wanting more. I save-scummed to experience all six endings, and getting a short cutscene felt like a bit of a letdown after investing 180 hours in such an incredible journey. Despite these minor complaints, the sheer freedom, beautiful art direction, and solid performance far outweigh the flaws. Whether you want to master a single weapon or replay the game ten times with ten different magic builds, there's plenty of room to experiment and enjoy yourself. Elden Ring lives up to the hype and is easily one of the best gaming experiences I've had. *Note: This review covers the base game only and does not include the DLC.*

Dead by Daylight has an amazing concept, iconic horror characters, interesting killer abilities, and so much wasted potential. Unfortunately, the experience for casual-beginers and returning players(after long time) can be absolutely miserable. You just want to enjoy a couple of matches after a long day, but instead you get matched against experienced players who know every map, every perk, and every trick in the book. The gameplay also gets incredibly repetitive. Repair generators, run, hide, get hooked, repeat. And here's my biggest complaint: WHY IS THERE STILL NO PROPER SINGLE-PLAYER MODE? I would happily play hundreds of hours against AI survivors and AI killers with adjustable difficulty, from Easy to Nightmare, proper progression, Bloodpoints, Prestige, and unlockable perks. I don't want to compete with strangers who spend their lives mastering every single mechanic. I want to enjoy the fantastic horror characters I've paid for, at my own pace. Yes, custom matches with survivor bots exist. But without proper difficulty settings, progression, rewards, or AI killers, they're no substitute for a real single-player experience. I want to win sometimes and not everytime play against professional flashlight enthusiasts and unbeatable killers. Until then, uninstalling. Maybe I'll see you next Halloween.

I'm surprised I never wrote a review for this game. I could just write "It's great. Buy it now." and that alone would be a valid review, but I'll go just a little further. If you've ever played the persona games and enjoyed making the most out of your time or wanted to be rewarded for planning ahead, this game is definitely for you. There may be some things that you can't plan for on your first playthrough until you find out they exist, but odds are you'll eventually want to start a new farm anyways, whether it be to try out different stuff, be more efficient, or check out something you may have missed the first time. HOWEVER, if you'd say you're more intrinsically motivated and do stuff just for the sake of it, that's fun too! I find the game intrinsically fun and it's made the game very replayable as a result. Unlike real life, doing just about ANYTHING can generate you money. Not all money-making methods are created equally of course, but you have options nonetheless. The music and atmosphere in this game is great too. The winter themes specifically are my favorites. There's also mod support, so you can make the game more fun by getting a modded farm layout, new NPCs, QoL mods, new crops, new areas, resprite characters, etc. Try the game out sometime, even if none of this may have sounded cool to you. There's quite a bit to do in this game with plenty of polish, and I recommend not playing with the wiki or anything until later and you've found yourself wanting to go beyond what you've already figured out. If that never happens and you just end up mining 24/7 because you find it funner than anything else, that's cool too! Unfortunately I don't find myself having the time to write as good of a review as I'd like, but hopefully this will do.

Praises: for a game from a triple A studio this game is filled with a dang good surplus of unique interactions, small details and Easter eggs to explore. The honor system allows different players to experience the game differently and gives good replay ability. Story is great with a good share of twists and good buildup, characters feel grounded and real. Lenny, Sally and Kieran are some of my personal favorite characters. and seeing the people slowly change over time as a response to the in game events is very fun. Also a good aspect of the game is that you can kill members of the KKK and the game rewards you with honor for doing that. Critiques: I do think it struggles a bit from having to many mechanics that aren't fully utilized outside of one or two quests to introduce them. But those introduction quests are at the beginning and all placed really close to each other making the mechanics feel crowded and overbearing to the new player. Satchel upgrades give incentive to engage with hunting but it never really felt that needed, I beat the game without a single one. Another critique is that like many other triple A games it suffers from a lot of character over crowding, Its another game where your character is already a member of a group and has been there for a long time, for that reason all of the individual members are thrown at you one after another and because your character is already canonically acquainted its hard to introduce the player to them in a natural way. Quests don't give time to expand on these characters individually instead having each mission play hot potato on who its focusing on and so most characters are hard to remember especially during the first half of the game. Also they killed online.

Cyberpunk 2077 is one of the greatest redemption stories in gaming history. What started as one of the most disappointing and rocky launches in recent gaming memory has evolved into an absolute masterpiece. It's genuinely incredible to see just how far this game has come. CD Projekt Red could have walked away, but instead, they put in the time, effort, and dedication to transform Cyberpunk 2077 into the experience it was always meant to be. Night City is absolutely breathtaking. It's one of the most immersive, detailed, and atmospheric open worlds I've ever experienced. Every street, alleyway, nightclub, and skyscraper feels like it belongs in a living, breathing world. The characters are unforgettable, the storytelling is phenomenal, and the choices you make carry emotional weight. The combat is incredibly satisfying, the customization is fantastic, and there's so much freedom in how you approach your build and playstyle. And then there's Phantom Liberty. Absolutely phenomenal DLC. This expansion is everything DLC should strive to be. The new storyline, characters, missions, atmosphere, and incredible performances elevate an already amazing game to another level. Dogtown is an incredible addition, and the storytelling genuinely rivals some of the best experiences in gaming. It doesn't feel like a small add-on; it feels like a substantial expansion that makes the entire experience even better. I would happily pay for more expansions of this quality. What impresses me most is the dedication CD Projekt Red showed in rebuilding this game. The updates, improvements, reworked systems, and continued support turned Cyberpunk 2077 into something truly special. It's a reminder that a rough launch doesn't necessarily have to define a game's entire legacy. I genuinely hope we get more stories, expansions, and opportunities to return to this incredible universe. Night City is a world I never want to leave, and I'd gladly spend another hundred hours exploring every corner of it. Cyberpunk 2077 went from a cautionary tale to a masterpiece. Phantom Liberty took it even further. An unforgettable experience, an incredible redemption story, and one of the best RPGs I've ever played. Never fade away! 11/01/2026

Playing this game was a mistake—because after finishing it, I feel like I’ve witnessed the absolute peak of gaming greatness, and nothing else will ever come close to this again. Especially while playing the Blood and Wine DLC, it felt overwhelmingly emotional. That subtle smile from Geralt at the very end—when he finishes talking to Regis and looks directly into the camera at you—leaves behind an emptiness best described as "Post-Witcher Depression." After spending well over a hundred hours meticulously crafting Grandmaster Griffin gear, completing every single contract and side quest, and living in a breathing world like Toussaint, it feels less like finishing a video game and more like coming to the end of a long personal journey. Blood and Wine isn't just an expansion; it is CD Projekt Red's royal farewell letter to Geralt and the players. After the dark, war-torn atmosphere of the base game and Hearts of Stone, stepping into the sunlit vineyards of Toussaint, experiencing the emotion of the fairytale realm, witnessing the sacrifice of a true friend like Regis, and finally finding a permanent home at Corvo Bianco is enough to make anyone emotional. In the history of fantasy RPGs, it is truly hard to find anything that matches the narrative depth and the soulful bond The Witcher 3 builds with its characters.
